Mr. GRAHAM moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 151) to provide for the adjudication of small claims arising in respect of the operation of the government railways. He said: The provisions of this Bill are, in short, to create of the Board of Railway Management a body that can be sued for small claims for damages, as they could be sued if they were a company, and that no fiat or petition shall be necessary before making such claims. There is a provision that under certain circumstances a ease may be removed to the Exchequer Court.
What is the limit of the claim?
Does it include actions for negligence, as well as undei contract?
Damages for negligence, but not under contract.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.
Before the orders of the day are called I would like to ask the Prime Minister whether he expects to make any announcement before the end of the session with regard to the Waterways treaty?

speechtext: All I can say is that I hope to be able to do so.

House resumed the adjourned debate on the motion of Sir Wilfrid Laurier for the second reading of Bill (No. 95) respecting the Naval Service of Canada, the proposed amendment of Mr. Borden thereto, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Monk.

Mr. Speaker, I believe we are face to face with a question which will have a greater bearing on the future prosperity, comfort, health, and wealth of the people of Canada than any other question that has been before this House, I was going to say, since confederation, but during the last decade. And, Sir, it is very gratifying to me, and it must be gratifying to every one, to know that both parties in this House are of one mind in regard to the great principle embodied in the Bill which is now before the House. As an evidence of that, I may cite the words of the hon. the Prime Minister, when he said that in case the supremacy of Great Britain on the high seas was endangered, it would be the duty of all the daughter nations to form a rampart around the motherland and protect her from attack; and in winding up his remarks, he said that the life of Canada depended on the safety of Great Britain, or words to that effect. And, Sir, those words were endorsed with stronger language by my own leader, the leader of the opposition.
What more significant event could there be than that which took place when, in one of the daughter nations, 3,000 miles removed from the motherland, 200 men, themselves descended from other lands, English, French, Irish, Scotch, German, and no doubt othersi, but citizens of the daugh-Mr. GRAHAM.
ter nation, elected as the representatives of the people in parliament, rose, not by concerted action, but as one unanimous whole, and sang together that national anthem of the motherland in honour of him who is every inch a king and every inch a man. But, Sir, how absurd it must have seemed to some of the neighbouring nations when they saw afterwards that some of the rabid partisans of both sides and some of the newspapers, probably looking for news, were crawling over each other in the effort to establish the claim that the national anthem belonged to them, that they were the only true, loyal party, that they were the only party that belonged to the motherland. This country is downtrodden, or will be, if we keep on in the way we are going. And the people will be over-ridden and depressed by combines and trusts, and I call upon the hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. King) at this juncture to add to the Bill which he has laid before the House this session a provision that there shall be no combine or trust in reference to the national anthem, the national flag or the loyalty of this country. That pernicious, avaricious, unpatriotic idea should be stamped out. Why cannot we all be of one mind with respect to that matter? In reference to the question of loyalty, my grandfather, when a young man, in 1776, left the state of Connecticut-and came to Canada to follow the flag. In 1812 he was one of the yeoman guards of the St. Lawrence river, repelling the American invasion, anl I take second place to no man with reference to my loyalty to the flag. Probably I know more than any one, excepting two hon. gentlemen in this House, when I say that there are no more loyal people than the sturdy yeomanry and mechanics of the riding from which I come. Who were more distressed, felt bluer or looked more so on the black days during the South African trouble than the men of Huron? Sir, it is easy enough in the large cities for young men to get together and enthuse and froth at the mouth in reference to loyalty, but when the scattered yeoman of the county from which I come came together and enthused in a patriotic way, as they did after the relief of Ladysmith and upon other notable occasions during the South African war, no one can require better evidence of their loyalty, and no overt act is needed. Outside the relatives of the men of the 42nd regiment, which was cut to pieces in South Africa, I do not believe there was a man in England who felt that event as keenly as did the people whose representative I am. I have been elected by the voters of West Huron to represent them in this parliament. This country is run by the larger of two parties, and it is impossible for all men of the different parties to think alike individual-
44.05

lv. Some have to give way to the others. It has been stated repeatedly in the Liberal press that the loyal opposition was divided on this question. I speak with knowledge when I say that there is no more division in the ranks of the opposition than there is in the ranks of the government. There are men on this side who will vote against their ideas and there are men on the other side who will vote against their ideas. There are Liberals who have been elected to follow the Liberal policy and to follow the Liberal party, and while they do not see eye to eye they will vote for their leader as we will vote for our leader. They would not ho doing their duty if they did not do so. I wish to note that I have been told by hon. members on both sides of the House, personal friends of mine, that if I publicly took the stand which I have taken privately I will not return to this House the next general election. If so I shall be sorry, but I trust my people will believe I acted in their interest as I believe I do.
Tell us what it is.

The hon. gentleman is asking me for information. There are two bad habits becoming prevalent in this parliament which tend to warp the dignity of parliament and interefere with the continuity of debate. One is asking questions which generally, like boomerangs, recoil on the persons who ask them. I have been very soTry at times to hear questions from this side of the House, because I felt that the person who asked them sometimes got the worst of it and vice versa. I am only going to speak for ten minutes, and if any person wants information I will be glad to give it to him, if I can, when I get through, but until then I do not want to be interrupted. One of the important features of the question before the House is what is the great pressing danger threatening the British empire. There is no doubt that the supremacy and life of the mother country rest entirely upon the $400,000,000 of toll which she receives for the carrying of the commerce of the world, and without which she could not stand for a moment. The main question is: How can we, as we have all agreed to do, help the mother country if she is in trouble? I do not think, from the documents which I have read and some of which I will hand into the House, that there is any pressing danger as far as Germany is concerned. Lord Beresford and Lord Roberts come out here and say there is. They have earned the right to say what they like, but they are men of war and they come out here and talk of war. The great canal man would come here and talk of canals, the great medical man would come and talk about tuberculosis or similar matters, but it rests 1401
with us to give consideration to all these views and help the country in the best way we can. I believe, Sir, that what Germany is preparing for is intervention by the United States in South America.
In support of this contention I give not my own opinion, but that of Captain Mahan, the greatest living naval expert who has declared that the German fleet is not unlikely to be used to establish a new state of things in Brazil or to dispute the control of the Panama canal. I also cite as an authority the Ottawa ' Citizen,' in which it was stated that the Germans are looking for a large tract of country in the Argentine republic, and Professor Schmoil-ler, a German, has declared that he looks forward to the day when there will be a second Germany of 30,000,000 people in southern Brazil. And, Sir, in this connection I would point out that the emigration to Brazil and to South America is of an entirely different class from that which comes to the shores of the northern part of this hemisphere. The German who comes to the land of the beaver or the land of the screaming eagle is rapidly assimilated into the population and becomes a supporter of the established institutions of these countries, but the German immigrant to South America is German, first, last, and always. But, Sir, notwithstanding the fact that there are experts who assure us there is no danger to England from the German menace, it is nevertheless the part of prudence to be prepared for war. As a recent editorial in the Toronto ' Telegram ' pointed out the unity of the British nations during the South African war prevented the terrible consequences of intervention by other nations, and the strength of the British fleet during the Spanish American war prevented intervention by Germany. The maxim is as true to-day as ever it was, that in time of peace we should prepare for war, and, Sir, the life blood of the British nation depends on the British fleet. The question then remains:	How can we as Canadians discharge our duty to the motherland. I say, Sir, that the solution is not to be found in the creation of a Canadian navy. Canada as a country is not ready for militarism, and God forbid that militarism should ever thrive in this peaceful land. I stand here taking my political ife in my hands to say, that I am unqualifiedly, unreservedly, and unconditionally opposed to regular militarism in Canada whether it is to be found in an army or in a navy. Of course, I do not include in that our militia system, but, I should be horrified to think that there would be imported into this country that militarism . which is the curse of some European countries and which can only end in officialism, red tape, circumlocution, poverty, and socialism. We have the evi-

dence at hand that our young Canadians will not join voluntarily-and they cannot be forced to join under our present happy conditions-the regular military service whether in the navy or in the army. I might point to the regular regiment at Halifax, which I believe is now only three-quarter strength, and I am told that 90 per cent of the men are British army pensioners. In a prosperous and growing country like Canada the young citizens of the country cannot be induced to give up their prospects and to tie themselves down to a life of idleness in the barrack room. For my part, I do not want to see in this country one-half the people working, slaving like the people in the old lands, keeping their noses to the grindstone, in order to support the other half in idleness preparing for a war which may never come. Then, I may be asked how do you expect to help the motherland? In a work entitled ' The A B C of the British navy,' prepared by Admiral Henderson and Mr. Bussell, it is pointed out that the great need of the British fleet is men. Lord Beresford has intimated to the British House of Commons that four-fifths of the British fleet is undermanned, that one-half of it had only the nucleus of crews, that one-fifth of the fleet only had its full compliment, and in a document which I shall lay on the table of the House for publication in ' Hansard.'
The hon. gentleman must read anything which he wishes to appear in ' Hansard.' The custom of the House is that anything that is to be published in' Hansard ' must be spoken or read.

Then, Sir, I will have to take up more time than I intended, and I regret having to do so, but I am in hopes that these citations may have some bearing on the question before the House. The literary digest, as quoted in the London ' Standard,' and the Hamburgher ' Nach-richten,' referring to the report of a German naval expert on the British navy says:
England's Half-manned Ships.
England at present, to judge from her parliamentary reports, is in a terrible condition of alarm over Germany's naval expansion. Each party blamed the other because ships with less than half crews had been ordered to sea. ' We have the ships, we have the men, we have the money too,' rang the old music-hall song. It is now admitted that England has the money, and can make as many shi,. . as she chooses, but the men are wanting. The present state of things we thus summarize from the London ' Standard ':-
The grave position of the home fleet is made plain in the details of its units as it assembles to-day off the mouth of the Thames for a cruise. Although it is composed of four squadrons, consisting in all of eleven battleships and fourteen cruisers, the startling fact Mr. LEWIS.
is disclosed that of these twenty-five vessels, fourteen are dangerously undermanned.
Of the undermanned vessels, six battleships have only half-crews; two of the cruisers have half-crews, while the remaining cruisers have only two-fifths crews.
Fourteen of the twenty-five ships, therefore, can not manoeuvre with the remaining eleven, can not fight, and can not run away. It is officially announced that this British war fleet is to exercise in the North Sea-where it will be subject to the keenest foreign criticism.
Commenting editorially on this avowal, the ' Standard ' observes:-
Such is the fleet which Mr. McKenna has sent to manoeuvre in the North Sea in winter. The useless hardship unnecessarily inflicted upon officers and men, the gratuitous waste of money, need no comment. But there are wider aspects of this incredible action to be considered. These are two. The first may be briefly indicated. At a time of somewhat critical international relations, the first lord sends to sea a fleet of t^venty-five ships whien an efficient squadron of half its size could sink or destroy, and the pitiable state of disorganization and weakness to which the^ British fleet has been reduced is advertised in the face of the whole world.
Of the keen foreign criticism which this London organ anticipates we may perhaps find a sample in the following remarks of the * Hamburger Nachrichten ':-
' It is not the ships but the men that do the fighting,' still remains the truest of dictums. And yet one often hears the question of a navy's strength or weakness decided merely by the number of its vessels-cruisers, battleships, torpedo boats, and submarines. As to the question of the number of her sailors, the recently formed reserve fleet is both undermanned and undertrained, but probably this will not be recognized until the moment of mobilization, which will result in its incorporation in the regular fleet. But what is very apparent is that in case of war Great Britain will suffer most from the insufficient manning of her own vessels.-Translation made for the ' Literary Digest,' March 27, 1909.
I cite the following from the Ottawa 'Citizen':
Men wanted in Navy-Ships are wasted for lack of Hands-Some have two-fifths of the Complement-Where will Crews be found for New Ships?
London, Oct. 25.-It has been stated officially that the battleships of the Albion class, which are to be stationed at the Nore as a reserve for the home fleet, are to be manned with reduced nucleus crews-that is to say, with about two-fifths of their full complements.	_
The ships of the Albion class-the Albion, Canopus, Glory, Goliath, Ocean, and Vengeance-though not large vessels, are very useful. They are of 12,950 tons, and carry-four 12-inch and twelve 6-inch guns, and are still capable of making eighteen knots when pushed. They have all been completed since 1900.
The Albions will join a number of ships

which are already laid up in reserve, manned with a fraction of their nominal complements.
The obstacle in the way of sending them to sea, however, is shortage of men.
Among the battleships which are laid up at the home ports in the third and fourth divisions of the home fleet are eight ships of the Majestic class-ships of 14,900 tons, armed with four 12-incli and twelve 6-inch guns and completed in 1895-8. These ships have- or are supposed to have- about three-fifths of their full complement on board, a large proportion of the short service men, who spend their years in the navy, principally in the ships, and are then passed into the reserve without any adequate training in the work of a sea-going fleet.
The ' Prince George,' of this class, is kept ' in dockyard hands,' for no other reason, apparently, than to save the cost of a crew.
Now, Sir, we have been told by the First Lord of the Admiralty in England that the preponderance of Great Britain in ships is so great that he absolutely refuses-I quote his own words to take over Bhips which are being built in England for foreign countries:
No Cause for Alarm-Britain is quite Safe-
First Lord of the Admiralty says the present supply of Dreadnoughts is Ample.
London, March 25, 1909.-Reginald McKenna, First Lord of the Admiralty, stated in the House of Commons that he declined to consider the advisability of purchasing one or other of the three Brazilian battleships now under construction in this country. He added:-
If we require more ships I think it would be better to build them ourselves, but we don't require any more ships at present. As regards the future, we will have ample time to build them.
I have some short citations here which 1 would like to have published in 'Hansard' without taking up the time of the House to read them.
I regret that I cannot grant permission to the hon. gentleman because it has led to abuses in the past. The 'Hansard' must be a report of what is said or read in the House.

Then, Sir, I trust that when the Prime Minister is revising the rules of the House he will make provision under which such citations as these may be printed without being read. Were such a rule in force it would in my opinion lead to a great saving of time. Let me point out, Mr. Speaker, that England is not wanting in ships at the present time. England is building a $40,000,000 navy for Spain, she is building three battleships for Brazil, she is building two for Chili, two ships for Italy, and other ships for other foreign countries, and under agreement with the builder the British government has the Tight to take these ships
at any time they are needed. We have, aff I have read, the refusal of the First Lord of the Admiralty to take these ships because he says they are not needed, and this would seem to establish good ground for my saying that England is not in need of ships. Now, Mr. Speaker, while I agree with the naval policy! of the government- (and in this I am speaking for mysel alone) with regard to building dry docks which are needed in this country, I absolutely disagree with them as to the building of a Canadian navy. As was said to me by a gentleman from the west, a man who knows the feeling of the people in the west as well as any other man in the House: Canada needs a navy just about as much as a man needs a fur overcoat in that land to which a good many of us are going hereafter.
Name.

Now, Sir, a word with regard to battle shins. If we looked at the history of the three last wars, the Chinese-Japanese war, the Russo-Japanese war, and the Spanish-American war, it will be seen that the naval strength of a nation depends on her battleships. In the A. B. C. of the British navy by Admiral Henderson and Mr. Russell, the dictum is laid down that the great final issue will be decided by the battleships alone; it was so at Trafalgar in days of hemp and wood; it is still so in the day of steam and steel. Therefore, Sir, if ships we are to have, it would seem that the best thing to provide are battleships, and together on the firing line. I cite that great family paper the Montreal ' Star ' :
The mobilization of a great British fleet of three hundred and fifty warships is a magnificent object lesson of the naval power of the empire. No such object lesson would appear if we were told that six British fleets were being mobilized-one in the home waters, another off Halifax, a third off Vancouver, a fourth near Australia, a fifth near New Zealand, and, possibly, a sixth under Table Mountain. Yet this division of the fleet and wide scattering of its power would be the logical outcome of the proposal to establish colonial navies.
The ' Free Press ' of Ottawa, on March 24, 1909, in an editorial headed ' Has Canada gone Batty also?' said:
We believe that the great body of public opinion in this country is against the idea of Canada being drawn into the vortex of European militarism.
The Huron ' Expositor,' Seaforth, Friday October 15, 1909:
The announcement is officially made that the imperial government of Germany will ask for a loan of $125,000,000, this enormous amount being required to cover deficits. This is one of the first fruits of intense militarism.

The common people are being ground to death to maintain an army and navy to gratify the vanity of the ruling elements and to provide positions for the sons of the aristocracy where they can have an affluent living at the expense of the toiling masses.
Now, Sir, how can we help the mother country? There is one way in which we can help her, and if the English experts knew it, they would at once grasp the idea. We have in this country 84,323 fishermen, the finest men that sail the waters, in the maritime provinces and on the great lakes, the descendants of those men who sailed the cutters of England and the luggers of France; and we have 11,490 sailors on the great lakes. I am sorry that we have not more sailors on the ocean, because we have hardly an ocean-going steamship or vessel under the Canadian flag. These men are busy in their vocation for six months in the year; and if you came with vessels of the type of the ' Charybdis,' and asked them to volunteer for a navy, you could not get one of them to leave his big pay and his prospects. But after their return on the first of December, and after they had their holiday of one month at home, this government on the second of January of each year could get 40,000 or
50.000	of these men-and I guarantee that I could get 5,000 from the shores of my own lake and 200 from my own town-sailors, stokers and engineers, to volunteer to go to Halifax or Vancouver and take three *months' training at the big guns; and I would suggest that this government do not buy any expensive warships, which will be scrap in a few years, but make an arrangement with the motherland under which she will send out a dozen or more men-o-f-war on which these young men can he trained. Canada to pay them. I will guarantee that after three years' training
40.000	young Canadians would be likely to give as good an accoant of themselves as the several thousand Canadians, Australians and New Zealanders who went to South Africa during the Boer war and there gave evidence of their loyalty. Why, Sir, the people of my county were tumbling over each other to get to the recruiting office in their desire to be taken to South Africa. We could have sent 10,000 from western Ontario in case the motherland got into trouble, to say nothing of the two or three hundred we did send. I also quote the words of the Earl of Clan William, in an interview with the Toronto ' News ' last July:
Canada would do a great service to the empire if it built up a reserve of seamen, who would be invaluable in case of war breaking out.
If the Admiralty were asked if they would prefer forty thousand sailors trained to big guns they would say yes. I Mr. LEWIS
say it advisedly, from investigations made by myself and by members on both sides of the House who have spoken to me on the matter, that I believe that four out of every five men in Ontario-and I have heard the same from other provinces-do not believe in a navy for Canada, and I believe there are more who are against a contribution to the motherland. Some people go wild on the subject of imperialism; but, Sir, there are threads of love and affection and friendship and sentiment uniting us to the motherland which, though fine as silk, are stronger than steel. But, Sir, if you are going to try to put handcuffs oi iron on the hands of the free Canadian citizen, and try to put him in an iron cage, those handcuffs will snap like thread. There is no overt act of loyalty required from a Canadian. We are always ready when the time comes. There is a definition of ingenuity which applies to the Canadian people-to do the right thing at the right time without being asked to do it. But, Sir, when you ask us to repay those bonds of love and friendship and kinship with money or with paid help, you are making a mistake. There is nothing like personal service in matters of this kind. In reference to the British men of war and the Canadian seaman, I cite the case of a present editor of the Toronto ' Globe,' Mr. Ewan, who was sent by his paper in 1899 down to the island of Newfoundland, to go round that island with the British fleet, which was trying the expedient of ascertaining what Newfoundland sailors were made of. They went from port to port and called the fishermen and sailors together and spoke to them. At first the men were averse to any questioning. Finally a large number, probably 2,000 or 3,000, volunteered for a voyage to the West Indies and back. They went and returned, and the British admiral was very much pleased with them, and they were pleased with their experience in handling the big guns. What was the result? The British admiralty sent out the ' Charybdis ' and tried to get men to volunteer for the whole year, but they found that it was an absolute impossibility. We are not ready for regular militarism in this country. Now, Sir, as to war: It is not a question of ships altogether- and I probably know more about it than most other members of this House, from my youthful training on vessels, though I have never been on a man-of-war-it is not a question of ships or of the number of men, but it is a question of the quality of the men. It is the man behind the gun. Drake's ships would not have roared so loudly or so strongly had they been manned by others than the seamen who did man them. Why cannot these two parties meet together on thi3 great question and do what is best under the circumstances? Both parties are asking Canada, which knows all about rail-

ways, to build battleships. We do not know anything about battleships, but we doJcnow that we have the best class of men to man them that can be found anywhere, and they are all from the same common stock Frenchmen and Englishmen, they all come from the same stock. I have it on the authority of a high personage in this House that when the Welsh sailors and fishermen, from which stock I am descended, and the French mariners from St. Malo, and other ports in the province of Normandy and Britany^St. Malo, famous as the point from which Jacques Cartier came originally-when these two nationalities meet in the channel on their fishing voyages, they speak to each other in the one mother tongue although parted for centuries. That shows conclusively that we are all descended from the one stock, and there should not be any division among us in this matter as regards loyalty. We ought all to be one in that sentiment.
I repeat that I am absolutely opposed to spending $25,000,000 for a Canadian navy or $25,000,000 for two Dreadnoughts. There are one million people who pay the taxes of this country, and that means a tax of $25 on every man of them. There is not one of them who will stand for it. It is not a question of going to the country. There are enough people in the country who would vote for men and not for measures, but if a plebiscite were taken, both the policy of the government, and the opposition would be defeated by an overwhelming majority.
Hi9 Majesty, King Edward, our sovereign, has by his wisdom, policy, and tact, earned the title of Edward the Peacemaker, yet still his battleships are being launched with increasing rapidity, each new one stronger than its predecessor in every thing that goes to making a fighting machine. And that supremacy pn the high seas, which England gained 300 years ago from Spain, has continued until this day, and has ever been the greatest safeguard to the peace of the world. I look to see the day when England and Celtic peoples shall be bound together in one harmonious whole-Gael and Gaul alike-for the peace of the world.

Under ordinary circumstances, I should feel almost like apologizing to the House for taking part in a discussion which has been so prolonged. But since I have the honour of a seat in this House, and while I have been endeavouring to attend to the discharge of the duties pertaining to that position to the best of my ability, I do not think I have trespassed upon the time of the House by over much, or over long speaking; and I might be permitted to say, without desiring to give offence to any one, that if some hon. gentlemen were to follow
my example in this respect, there would not be such necessity for revising the rules of the House. In this matter, however, I feel that I would not be doing justice to myself or those I represent were I to give a silent vote. The question we are discussing is probably the most imnortant that has come before parliament since confederation. It involves an entirely new departure. It means the inauguration of an entirely new policy, rendered necessary by the increased prosperity and influence of this country, and its increased attachment to the empire.
I have no very great objection to many of the remarks which have been made by my hon. friend and good neighbour from West Huron (Mr. Lewis) who has just spoken, and consequently I do not intend attempting to make any particular answer to any particular point he has raised; but there are some things on which he has dwelt to which perhaps I shall refer as I proceed. But at the outset, let me say that I do not intend to treat this question from a technical, scientific, or even constitutional standpoint. Technically I know very little about it, but I shall endeavour to deal with it from a plain, practical, common sense point of view. In my opinion, having regard to the very great importance of this subject, it is necessary that the people in every constituency should be seized of all the conditions, and the only way which they can get that information is through the discussion in this parliament. Consequently I feel that any discussion on this matter is not by any means time wasted. As I have said I intend to deal with it from a plain, practical, common sense standpoint, and the question before the House, stripped of all superfluity, may be reduced to a very plain, practical, easily understood proposition. In the first place, the opposition propose that a large sum of money be donated to Great Britain for the purpose of enabling her to improve and extend her navy, Great Britain to continue the expense and the responsibility of the naval protection of Canada, and the money which we give to Great Britain to' be expended in that country for the benefit of British ship builders and artisans. On the other hand the proposition of the government is that a lesser amount of money be devoted towards the establishment or erection of the nucleus of a Canadian navy for the protection of our own shores, thus relieving Great Britain of the expense and responsibility of the naval protection of this country, and this money to be expended in our own country for the benefit of Canadian ship builders and artisans and also for the purpose of building up a larger shipbuilding industry in Canada which will give

employment to thousands of our working people and enlarge the home market for our farmers and manufacturers. It is quite proper that I should say that our love for and devotion to the mother country is only right and proper. Filial affection, I am sure, is one of the noblest traits of human nature; but filial affection divorced from self-preservation does not amount to a very great deal. It is the boy, the young man, which makes the best use_ of his opportunities and the gifts with which he has been endowed, and who shows a disposition to carve out his own future and to paddle hi3 own canoe who is always dearest to the mother's heart. And, Sir, if Canada shows a disposition to take advantage of the great privileges which have been placed in her way, of the great natural advantages with which she has been endowed, and if she shows a disposition to take care of herself and do what is right and necessary in her own interest, she will, I contend, do that which is most likely to win the esteem and confidence and trust of the people of Great Britain and of every other country.
Sir, I was sorry to notice, whether consciously or unconsciously, running through nearly every speech of hon. gentlemen opposite, a vein deprecatory of Canada and of Canadians.
Oh, no.

Yes; we had it stated here, over and over again, that Canadians have not the ability nor the skill to construct their own ships. We have had Australians held up to us as a bright and shining example because she has sent her money to- Great Britain and looks to Great Britain to construct her ships. We have heard, in almost every speech from the opposite side of the House, attempts made to detract from the honour and credit which is due to the right hon. the leader of this House (Sir Wilfrid Laurier). Attempts have been made, time and time again, to show that he is disloyal to his country, that he has betrayed the trust which was reposed in him by the people, and that he is not acting in good faith with the people,and soon and so on; and, lastly, that he is introducing a policy which is simply the thin end of the wedge of disruption of the empire. One hon. member-I think it was the hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. Cowan)-spoke for two mortal hours here the other night, and at least one-third of his speech was devoted to that sort of thing. Sir, the name and memory of Sir Wilfrid Laurier will remain bright and green in the minds and hearts and affections of the people of Canada long after the hon. member (Mr. Cowan) and I are forgotten. We have also had a brilliant word-picture placed before us showing Great Mr. M. Y. McLEAN.
Britain at war with Germany; her immense fleets were assembled upon the high seas; the word went forth to Australia and she came forward courageously and promptly with her fleet unit: the word went forth to little New Zealand and she came forth, with equal promptitude, with her Dreadnoughts: the word went forth to Canada, and she came up at the heel of the hunt with her ' tin pot navy.' And when the great British admiral cast his eye over his assembled fleet as they rode the sea ready for action, he looked upon Australia and beamed upon her with pleasure and pride; he looked upon New Zealand and she equally met with his approval; he looked upon Canada, he frowned upon Canada, and ordered her to the rear and instructed her to sail for her own shores as fast as her ships could carry her: and poor Canada had neither part nor lot in the bloodless conflict of that picture. When I heard all this, it seemed to me that the author of it should have been a novelist instead of a politician. I ask: When has Canada undertaken any great national enterprise and has not carried it out successfully? Have not Canada's sons, in almost every department of life and in every country of the world, signalized their ability and proven their integrity and uprightness and every characteristic which goes to make a good, a worthy, a proper man? Wherever the sons of Canada have come into competition with the people of other countries, have they not almost invariably come to the front? If there is one thing more than another for which I am truly thankful it is that I am a Canadian. I am proud of Canada, and proud of Canada's sons; and I have not the least hesitation in saying that, should Canada undertake to construct a navy, she will have a navy that will be a credit to her at home and abroad. And should this country, unfortunately, be dragged into a war either at home or abroad, I for one do not doubt that Canada's sons will acquit themselves with the same prowess, the same bravery that has distinguished them and given them a name in every country of the world. In view of the facts, I say that it is not fair, it is not manly, for hon. members opposite to endeavour to cover their veiled insinuations against Canada by loud protestations of loyalty to the mother country.
But there is something else that should be said. I believe it is the duty of every true Canadian to preach, and, in so far as he can, to practise the doctrine of peace and not the doctrine of war. For the future of this great and growing and grand country depends upon the farm and the factory and not upon the sword or the battleship.
I notice that in nearly every speech hon. gentlemen opposite profess disappointment with the provisions of the Bill now before the House on the ground that it is not

comprehensive enough, that it does not go far enough. I, too, am disappointed, but I am agreeably disappointed; for,
I am free to confess, I did have a lingering fear, if I might so express it, that the government would ask this House to commit the country to an elaborate scheme requiring an immediate expenditure of millions of money which, I think, could be more profitably devoted to developing the latent resources of the country. I therefore say that it is a fortunate thing for Canada that we have in power at this time a government, and more particularly a prime minister, with the stamina and courage to resist this wave of jingoism which seems to be passing over the country, and to refuse to do unwise and foolish things which afterwards the people might regret for many years to come. No person dreads war, or is more opposed to militarism, than I am. And I think it does not say much for the Christian civilization of the twentieth century when the civilized nations of the world cannot come together and agree on some more rational and sensible means of settling their disputes than in wasting their money in armaments and their efforts in killing one another. But we must take conditions as we find them. And we find that the nations of the world have not yet reached what we might call the ideal point, when they can settle their disputes upon a rational and sensible basis and in a manner which would be a credit to the integrity and character and intelligence of the country. Until such is the case, we must meet conditions as we find them. And I am free to confess that, in my judgment, the time has come in the history of Canada when it is necessary that we should make some fitting preparation to meet the requirements of the country in this direction.
Such a time does come I think in the history of almost every country and every nation, and it comes to a lesser extent even to municipalities. For example, for a village or a town one policeman is ample for the purpose of maintaining peace and order within that municipality; but when that town grows to become a large, populous and influential city, a whole regiment of policemen are required. So it is with Canada. If I may be allowed to use the expression, Canada has emerged from the town stage to the large, prosperous and influential city stage, and consequently it is necessary that some provision should be made such as is now proposed. I would not have been disappointed, in fact possibly I would have been rather pleased, if the government had seen fit to adopt a smaller plan than that which is proposed. But there is not sufficient difference between them to justify a difference of opinion, as both are practically the same in principle. But I believe in making this provision, we should commence on a modest scale such as the government proposes, and that we should allow the enterprise to grow in strength as the country grows in strength, power, wealth and influence. Also, I think that what we do should be done under the direction of Canada, and should remain entirely under the control of Canada. And we should take very great care indeed not to allow this country to become in any way entangled or mixed up with old world troubles or difficulties. What I mean is that we should keep Canada in this position, that if even Great Britain should engage in a war of which we did not approve, the justice and righteousness of which we were not convinced of, this country should stand aloof, as we have done on other occasions, and act the part of a looker-on. But if, on the other hand, Great Britain became engaged in a war of self defence, or for any interest of humanity, or for purposes which appealed to our sympathies and our sense of right, then we should join in and help Great Britain even to the extent of our last dollar and our last man.
I also believe that whatever we do should be done entirely in the interest and for the benefit of Canada, and not in payment of any supposed debt which we owe the mother country. Now the idea has pervaded the speeches of many hon. members opposite, and especially the speech of the hon.- member for North Toronto, that Canada is in some way materially and morally indebted, even immensely indebted, to Great Britain, and that this proposed donation is in payment of that supposed debt. Now, Sir, I am not in the habit of proclaiming my loyalty from the house-tops, but I take no second place to any man in my loyalty to Great Britain, the birth-place and home of my forefathers. But, Sir, I am a Canadian, I am loyal to Canada first, last and all the time; and I think that at the present time perhaps a little plain speaking on this subject might not do any harm. I say this claim of our hon. friends opposite that we are greatly indebted to Great Britain is a fallacy which cannot be supported by fact. As a Canadian, I wish to say that in a material sense we are not indebted to Great Britain for anything, and in no' sense is Canada indebted to her for more than good will and filial affection. If I desired to establish that point, I think I could do so by a few words which fell from the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) in the concluding part of his address in this House. I understand that that hon. gentleman is the leader of the Conservative party of the great province of Quebec; I know he is a deputy leader of hon. gentlemen oppo-

site. So long as he is their leader, they are responsible for his utterances until they repudiate his leadership. I have not heard that they have endeavoured in any sense so far to repudiate his leadership, and I think they dare nor do it; consequently they are responsible for his expressions in this House and elsewhere as their political leader.
Now, Sir, I would like to 'bring the minds of hon. gentlemen opposite down from the realm of pure sentiment in which some of them so much delight to dwell, to plain facts, every day facts. If I can do this, they will find that Canada has never received one dollar from Great Britain for which sjje has not given a good big dollar's worth in return. It may be said, and it has been said in this House, that Great Britain furnishes us our best market for our surplus products. That is quite true, but it is equally true that this is a mutual obligation, because Great Britain requires our products just as much as we require her market. And she has never given us the fraction of a cent more for our products, for our apples, our cheese, our butter, our bacon, our bullocks, our cereals, than she could get them for elsewhere, or because they were Canadian. On the contrary, she has persistently, for years, _ maintained against this country a barrier to our live stock going into her markets. Now remember I do not blame her for this. If she considers such a policy in the interest of her own people she has a perfect right to pursue that policy, and we have no right to complain. But what I want to point out is this, that Great Britain adopts the policy which she considers in the interest of her own people, irrespective of the results which it may have upon Canada; and so I say in that respect as well as in other respects we should follow her example. It has always been said in this House and throughout the press of this country that most of our great national enterprises are carried on by means of British capital. That is quite true, but it is equally true that we have never borrowed one dollar from Great Britain for which we have not given her the highest current rate of interest and the very best security. It is equally true that she has never loaned us a dollar upon better or more favourable terms than she has loaned to other countries.
But, Sir, the most silly contention I think I have ever heard made in this House is that she has protected our shores from invasion by foreign foes. Now I ask when, in the memory of living man, have our shores been even threatened by a foreign foe? The only occasion I remember is what was known as the Fenian Kaid, and that was not inspired by any Mr. M. Y. McLEAN.
dislike for Canada but by a dislike for Great Britain, because she denied to a certain portion of her subjects the rights and privileges which they thought, and which I think, they were justly entitled to. The last contention along that line that I shall refer to is that she has protected^ our commerce on the high seas. That is also quite true, but it is equally true that any protection she has afforded to Canada in that way has been purely incidental. She has protected her own breadstuffs and she has afforded to Canada in that respect the same protection that slm has afforded to other countries and nations from which she has drawn these breadstuffs. I do not give these illustrations in the way of complaining that we have not received just and proper treatment from Great Britain. On the contrary, I give them to show, in the interest and in defence of Canada, that Canada has done her whole duty to the mother country, that she has not played the part of a sponge 'absorbing everything and giving out nothing.
Let me refer for a moment or two to the amendment which has been placed before this House by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden). I think we can divide it into three parts very properly and justly. In the first place, it is proposed that Canada should bestow on the mother country a gift of from $22,000,000 to $25,000,000; secondly, that a real emergency exists by reason of the' danger of war between Great Britain and Germany, and thirdly, that Canada should provide a navy of her own, but that before she does so she should take a plebiscite of the people. Now let me consider each one of these proposals, made by our friends opposite, separately. The first is that Canada should bestow on the mother country a gift of from $22,000,000 to $25,000,000. Why, in all that is sensible, should Canada give to the mother country any such sum? If the mother country were in need of this money, if she were in stress, then I say that it would be quite right and proper for Canada to give her that money, and it would be the duty of "Canada to do so. But, is the mother country in need of money? No, as the boys say,, she has money to bum. From the money standpoint she could buy out Canada twenty times over and that being the case why should we in this House vote the hard earned money of the labourer, the artisan, the farmer, the merchant and the manufacturer of this country to fill the already over-flowing coffers of Great Britain? I do not think we would be justified in doing anything of the kind, because there is no necessity for it._ Now, let us come to the second proposition that an emergency exists. In order to prove their case hon. gen-

tlemen opposite must, of necessity, prove that an emergency does exist, and if they fail to do so, in my humble judgment, their whole case falls to the ground. How have they gone about proving an emergency exists? They have quoted from the speeches delivered by British statesmen over a year ago, speeches that were delivered for an election and for political purposes and also for the purpose of bringing the British people to a realization that they had not been keeping up their navy ro the standard which it formerly had been kept up to, and that it was necessary to provide funds for that purpose. That, Sir, was the object, and in these respects it has been realized. The emergency has passed over, the scare is no more, and now only exists in the minds of hon. gentlemen opposite. But, Mr. Speaker, who is it that they have sought to show that Great Britain has really to be afraid of? Afraid of Germany. Why should she be afraid of Germany? Are not the ties of kinship as well as of commerce, against any such proposition? Is not Great Britain one of Germany's very best customers? Is not Germany one of Great Britain's very best customers? Why then should Germany desire to destroy her best customer? It is said that Germany is rapidly increasing her navy. That is quite true, but it is necessary that she should increase her navy just the same as it is necessary for France, or Austria, or Japan, or other surrounding countries to do so. She was obliged by that necessity to do it, and it was not for the purpose of going to war with Great Britain. Let me tell you that the Germans are not a foolish people, the Germans are not a people who are foolish enough to bite off their noses to spite their faces. They are an intelligent, hard-headed, frugal, enterprising, law-abiding people and they know too well upon which side their bread is buttered to instigate a war with Great Britain or with any other country that they are so dependent upon as they are dependent upon Great Britain at the present time. There is a word that I would like to say here if the House will pardon me for a short digression. I was very much pleased and delighted at the intimation which my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) gave to the House the other day, that the little commercial war which had been in existence between Canada and Germany for a few years had been closed up and that a truce had been proclaimed. I was not pleased so much on account of the improvement in the commercial relations that that would accomplish, or the commercial advantages that might accrue to Canada from that, although I have no doubt they will be very considerable, but I think it will have a strong tendency to encourage immigration from Germany to Canada, and we cannot get a better class of immigrants from any country in the world than we can from Germany. It has been proved in this country time and time again, and any of us who have German settlers in our constituencies know how valuable these settlers are in the cities, towns, villages and communities, in which they live throughout this province without any other evidence. They are an industrious, well-doing, enterprising, law-abiding people and we cannot get Canada populated with a better class than the German people. Now let me come to the third part of the amendment, that Canada should provide a navy of her own, but before she does so should take a plebiscite of the people. I do like consistency, but I am sure there is no consistency in thB position taken by the leader of the opposition in this amendment. He is quite willing that $25,000,000 of the money of the people of this country should be given to Great Britain right off the reel, without a word, for the benefit and advancement of the people of that country. But, Sir, when it comes to devoting a smaller sum of money to the development of the manufacturing industries of this country for the purpose of constructing a navy for our own protection, for the protection of our own shores, the whole of which money will be expended in this country, then forsooth, we must go to the country and ask for the consent of the people. As far as I can judge the amendment of my hon. friend was moved simply for the purpose of gathering in the stray lambs of the flock and herding them into one fold on the division. An hon. friend remarks that there are no lambs in that flock. Perhaps they are all grown sheep. If we really desire to aid Great Britain, and if we could aid her I think it is right and proper that we should do so. I think that we could do this much more effectively by helping ourselves, by devoting every dollar that we can raise to the development of the great natural resources of this country, by extending, improving and increasing our traffic highways to the sea-board and from the sea-board across the Atlantic, so that we can lay down our products in the British markets, and her products in our markets in the least possible time, in the best possible condition, and at least possible cost. We should provide profitable investments for the immense horde of surplus capital in Great Britain, and we should provide comfortable homes for the teeming millions of her population. These are the ways in which I think we could aid Great Britain much more effectively, much more to her interests as well as to our own interest, than by presenting her with Dreadnoughts, which, by the time they are constructed, will, in ail probability, be fit for the scrap heap,

^or which there is no necessity. In this way, I think we should work and build up on this continent a great nation which will be at least the equal, if it does not surpass, the greatest of the great nations of the civilized world. A nation that will work in harmony and consonance with the old mother who will look with pride and pleasure justly upon her brightest and best sons. This, Mr. Speaker, is an ambition worthy of young Canada. This, Sir, is an ambition which is worthy of our best energy, and our best intellect, and we have the men to accomplish it. Let us set ourselves to this work, and do it to the very best of our ability, and let us place this country of ours in the position which nature has destined her to occupy. And, Sir, if we do this, if each one of us does his duty, we need not trouble ourselves very much about difficulties between Germany and Great Britain. Why, thirty-five years ago, or possibly a little more, we had a similar scare to this. We had then precisely the same arguments which are to-day being used by hon. gentlemen opposite and notwithstanding all that, no trouble and no war between Germany and Great Britain has supervened in all these years. On the contrary, these two great countries have worked hand in hand together, and in trading with each other peacefully, they both have made profit, while advancing their own interests. Under such circumstances is it not a craven and cowardly thing for hon. gentlemen opposite, to be going up and down this country whining that Great Britain is afraid of being swallowed up by Germany. This is a species of loyalty which we on this iside of the House, at all events, do not profess.

I have listened to most of the speeches which have been delivered on the question before the House, and I cannot but feel that this parliament is now dealing with a measure of unparalleled importance in the history of Canada. There are three things which present themselves for our consideration as Canadians; the first is: the consolidation of the British empire; the second is: the maintenance of that empire, the greatest the world has known; and the third is the question as to what best we can do to bring about peace among the nations of the world. It is well, Sir, that we should consider this question free from personal or party bitterness and controversy I could- not help but think this afternoon, in listening to the speech of the hon. member for South Huron (Mr. McLean) that his language did not express, the sentiments of the people of his riding. He has talked a great deal about autonomy, as most hon. gentleman on his side have done, and in this connection I would like him to explain the relation between paragraph 4 Mr. M. Y. MCLEAN.
of this Bill and paragraph 18. It would be a great comfort to members on this side of the House if hon. gentlemen opposite would reconcile these features of the Bill, the one with the other. Section 4 of the Bill dis tinctly states, as does clause 15 of the British North America Act, that the Canadian navy shall be placed under the control of the King, but section 18 of the Bill just as distinctly states that the government of Canada shall have control of the navy and that they need not send it to war unless they wish to do so. This seems a contradiction. Then again, gentlemen opposite have been telling us that they are greatly in favour of peace throughout the world. The Minister of Labour, speaking in Harvard University hoped to see the day when the government of Canada and the government of the United States would join in building a monument on the border line to celebrate 100 years of peace. On the 8th of July last, the Prime Minister endorsed that suggestion of his Minister of Labour, and on the same day, speaking in Plattsburg, New York, the Postmaster General used this language:
Sir, is this not the fittest occasion to proclaim our determination that now on and forever the American Commonwealth and the Dominion of Canada shall always promote and advance the cause of peace, harmony and civilization on this vast continent.
There are heroes of peace as there are heroes of war, under different flags we are pressing towards a single goal-freedom, righteousness and duty.
But, where is that hero of peace to-day? Did we not find him a few weeks ago urging his compatriots to furnish the money to build a Canadian navy, which by the way I may say would be of no use to Canada for her own defence and of no service to Great Britain in time of war. I quote the words of the Postmaster General from 'Hansard ':
Why should we not have a navy as we have an army? The Canadian militia began fifty years ago; it is now a fighting force. May I not prophesy the same happy results for the Canadian navy.
Are we to understand from the Postmaster General that fifty years hence we will have a fighting force, in our navy? Well, it is quite possible that half a century in the future the Canadian navy, as proposed in this Bill, may be of some consequence. Then again, the Postmaster General says:
We must exhibit our fighting qualities and take care of ourselves against the United
States.	*
And the member for Huron (Mr. McLean) gives his hearty approval to such language. Are we to say to the people of the United States: Wait a little longer until

Canada has built a fleet, wait until we have abrogated the Rushe-Bag-ot treaty and built our cruisers on the great lakes? Is that what hon. gentlemen opposite would wish as the outcome of this navy? I can tell the Prime Minister that the United States ship builders would only be too glad to see the abrogation of the Rushe-Bagot treaty so that they might build on the great lakes war ships and naval armament. And, Sir, does the protection of our shores only mean the Atlantic and Pacific coast line, are we not to take into consideration all oi the 7,600 miles of shore line which we have in this Dominion? On the eastern coast we have 3,000 miles of shore line between the United States boundary and Hudson straits; on the west we have 1,000 miles oi coast line between the United States boundary and Alaska, and in addition we have 3,600 miles of boundary line between the United States and Canada. When you take into consideration that most of our wars have come from the United States, one can readily understand that in preparing for coast defence it is necessary also to take into consideration preparation for the de fence of the boundary line between Canada and the republic to the south. It must be remembered that were England to be engaged in a war with Germany, there are
16,000,000 Germans in the United States who would not sympathize with the Monroe doctrine being enforced on the northern half of this continent. Then, have we no1 some duty to protect our mercantile marine? When we realize that 70,000,000 tons of water-borne freight passes through the Clair river every year, and that a large portion of it is carried by Canadian merchant marine, we must also realize that that merchant marine demands protection.
When we realize that we own half of this continent, with seven millions of people scattered over its length and breadth, we must see that with our limited resources it would be perfect folly on our part to attempt to protect all our boundary line. Have not the people of Sarnia, Goderich, Sault Ste. Marie, Port Arthur and many other prominent cities on our great lakes just as good a right to expect shipyards and dockyards to be built in them as many of the cities on our eastern and western coasts? If we enter upon a career of navy building, as proposed by this government, we will have no end of competing cities on our coasts all wanting to build ships of war. If we pass this Bill we enter on a mad race for naval construction, and commit our people to an indefinite, perpetual and ever-draining policy. The Canadian people are a patriotic people, proud of their homes, their lands and their progress. They do not shrink from assisting the motherland; but I do not believe that they are anxious to undertake the expenditure which this government is proposing for the
purpose of building a navy, especially one that will not be of any definite help to Great Britain. The defence of the empire is not the defence of the British islands alone, but includes the defence of Great Britain's colonies and dependencies. The Prime Minister may well say that when Great Britain is at war, Canada is at war, because the only hope of Canada remaining a part of the British empire depends upon Great Britain having the command of the sea. If Great Britain were defeated in a war, of what good would be all this talk about autonomy and having the rights of the people of Canada protected? I am absolutely opposed to militarism in every sense of the word; but I realize that there is only one court of appeal to which nations can go at present, and that court is war. However, I sincerely hope' and believe that the day is not far distant when the nations of the world will come together in a bond of peace and submit their differences to a court of arbitration similar to the Hague tribunal, and war will be no more. Only a few weeks ago I received a letter from a Mr. Marburg, in the city of Baltimore, at whose home a conference was held a few nights previous at which a large number of prominent citizens of the United States were present. At the conference a plan of campaign was mapped out for this continent and the different nations of Europe to educate the people up to a sense of their duty on this question of peace. The President of the United States, Senator Root and many other prominent men have given their hearty approval to the project. Within the next few months we may expect to see a propaganda started for the holding of public meetings in the United States and in Canada to urge the people to assist in bringing about a cessation of the mad rush for armaments on the part of the nations of the world. I sincerely trust that whatever can be done in the wav of assisting this movement will be done by the men of Canada. Until we are able to build a navy worthy of the name, or until international peace is consummated, it would be folly for us to undertake to build such a navy as is proposed by this^ government. The proper position for us is to stand by the British navy. On this occasion there is a distinct line of cleavage between the two great political parties of this country. The opposition say: submit the question to the people Snd give two Dreadnoughts to tide over the present emergency. If you look into the records of Great Britain, Germany or the United States you will find that it takes years to build Dreadnoughts, and if we placed at the disposal of Great Britain the money proposed by the hon. leader of the opposition in his resolution, it would probably take two years or more before I the battleships would be ready to go into service.
