time of need, wasting money in building a useless navy that can be of no service to Canada or Great Britain. England's nvay is closely associated with her greatness, with the mighty deeds which have extended her empire and made her mistress of the seas. The British fleet to-day, centred as it is around Great Britain, is within striking distance of Canada. We must remember the fact that within five days of our shores is the British fleet, practically as near to Canada as the eastern portion of Canada is to British Columbia. Wireless telegraphy and cables render the protection of our Shores by the British fleet more effective than they would be by a separate squadron. Australia and New Zealand, lying as they do at a greater distance, require an entirely different system of defence. We have no enemies excepting the enemies of Great Britain. And we must remember this fact, that our people are not only self-reliant and confident, a people full of energy and hope, but they are a people willing and ready to contribute of their means towards assisting Great Britain in time of crisis. We may make -mistakes in the legislation that comes before this parliament, mistakes which we can remedy, but, in forcing this Bill through parliament, we shall make a mistake in imperial policy which will be irretrievable. The colonies have been the cause of most of Britain's wars, and while Britain owns one-fifth of the land area of the globe, and controls a quarter of the world's population, it will be necessary for her to have a large army and a large navy.
We cannot but admire the justice with which Great Britain has governed her overseas dominions. She has displayed unflinching confidence and absolute justice in dealing with Canada, not only with the French Canadians of Canada, -but with every other nationality, since she has put them all on the same footing. She extends the same square dealing to all her colonies and dependencies; justice in administration is always the uppermost aim in England's administration. Then England is the greatest importer in the world. She imports food and raw material for her population, and she exports manufactured goods. Seven-eighths of her imports are food and raw material, and seven eighths of her exports are manufactured articles. To keep the British empire together, we must first protect her commerce, and this is done by helping her to keep command of the sea. We hear much said about the necessity of protecting our commerce on the high seas. In that connection I would like to read an extract from a report of the Royal Commission on Food Supply in Time of War. This commission was appointed in 1905, and we find that many of the most prominent men of England were on that commission. At the Mr. ARMSTRONG.
head of it was His Royal Highness the Prince of Wales, and among the members were the Rt. Hon. Lord Balfour of Burleigh, His Grace the Duke of Sutherland, the Rt. Hon. Lord Berkeley, the Rt. Hon. John Henry Chapman, and many others. Now let us see what this commission has to say with regard to Great Britain's food supply in time of war, and the protection of that food supply. Here is what they say in the course of their report:
The imports of wheat aDtl flour in 1904, given in millions of quarters, were as follows: United States of America, 4 -40; Russia, 5 -53; Roumania, -35 ; Argentina, 5-10 ; British India, 5-95; Canada, 2 13; Australia, 2-65; minor exporting countries, 1 -59.
So when we hear hon. gentlemen opposite talking about sending to Great Britain the whole of her food supply, they must take into consideration the fact that India sent to Great Britain in 1904 double the amount of wheat that Canada did. The report gives the various sources of Britain's food supply as follows:
The supplies from the principle sources begin to arrive as follows: January, wheat from the Pacific coast of America; February and March, Argentine wheat; April, Australian wheat; May, June and July, Calcutta and Bombay, Delhi and Karachi Indian wheats; July and August, American winter wheat ; September and October, American spring and Russian wheat; November, Canadian wheat.
This goes to show that Great Britain has practically a supply from various sources all the year round, one source or another every month, as I have just shown. On page 28 of this report we have some very important facts:
In their communications to us the admiralty admit that the policy of attacking the floating trade of a country has always played an important part in maritime warfare. But in a summary of the events of the various maritime wars of the 17th, 18th and 19th centuries they point out that naval history demonstrates the truth of these two general principles.
I would ask your consideration to this, Mr. Speaker:
1.	That the command of the sea is essential for the successful attack or defence of commerce and should therefore be the primary aim.
2.	That the attack or defence of commerce is best effected by concentration of force, and that a dispersion of strength for either of those objects is the strategy of the weak, and cannot materially influence the ultimate result of the war.
And, surely, Mr. Speaker, if the right hon. gentleman who leads this House would consider the statements of these men, made in 1905, when there was no general election on in Great Britain, and

would apply their suggestions to the case of the Canadian navy, he would see that the policy he is undertaking is named by them, 'the stategy of the weak', and they say that it 'cannot materially influence the ultimate result of a war'. They emphasize this further on page 30 of the report:
We were specially anxious on this point, on account of the evidence warning us that we must expect captures, and we asked the following questions:-
(1) Assuming the country to he at war with any two of the great maritime powers, are the admiralty of opinion that onr supplies of wheat and flour would arrive in practically the same volume as they come at present?
. . . Practically, the reply is yes, as the admiralty believe that there would he no material diminution in the supplies of wheat and flour reaching the United Kingdom.
The question and answer in this report proceed:
(4) Supposing popular pressure took the form of demand for more direct defence of our food supplies, and special protection of ships carrying foodstuffs to this country than the naval authorities would otherwise contemplate, and was successful, do the hoard consider the probable result would prejudice arrangements for the general conduct of our offensive operations of war against the hostile fleets?
The answer to that is as follows:
If a portion of the naval forces at the disposal of the admiralty were deflected from the main operations of the war for other purposes of whatever kind, the general conduct of these operations must of necessity suffer, and the entire course of the war might be injuriously affected.
Just the very thing the present government are doing is the thing which the British admiralty and this commission most- emphatically state should not be done. Another statement is as follows- page 32:
The number of British merchant steamers which would be taken up by the government in war time is so small compared to the total number available that it is not believed the British carrying trade could he seriously interfered with. The admiralty have already been in consultation on the subject with some of the leading shipowners.
Sir Cyprian Bridge also thought that if proper naval arrangements were made, the losses by capture, or by ships being driven on shore, of vessels bringing imports into the United Kingdom, would not exceed a very small percentage of the total, and he suggested that the proportion lost would probably amount to about 5 per cent.
So, if this government are building their navy for the purpose -of protecting our merchant marine, it is easy to see what folly it is. And what do these gentlemen say as regards torpedo craft?
It should be added that torpedo-craft (i.e., destroyers and torpedo boats) can neither 141
spare prize crews nor accommodate any one above their complement numbers. If, therefore, employed against commerce, for which they were never intended, such craft could only compel merchant ships to follow them into port under threat of being torpedoed. Moreover these crafts can only operate within a comparatively short distance of their shore bases.
I think that is sufficient at least to call your attention to the fact that, so far as the navy proposed bv this government is concerned, it is utterly inadequate and can be of no service for the protection of our merchant marine. The government talk about protecting our commerce. Let us, for a moment, take the United States as an example. Out of the port of Baltimore went 50,000,000 bushels of grain last year of which only 10,000 bushels were carried in American bottoms. Out of the port of New York last year went 1,200 ships, and of these only seven carried the American flag. If you investigate the commerce of the United States you are forced to the conclusion that they are not building their navy for the protection in particular of their own commerce. They are in an altogether better position as concerns population and consumption than we are. It seems utter nonsense, therefore, for us at the present time, with our small population and small income, to attempt to build a navy such as would adequately protect our commerce.
War is organized force. When peace is broken the nation best organized and prepared for war has the best chance of defeating its opponent. Only men make war, and it is a well-reasoned affair and conducted on business principles. Germany, when she defeated France, demanded from France a thousand million of dollars of indemnity. What would be the indemnity Germany would demand of the British empire if she defeated that empire on the high seas? Instead of a thousand millions, the indemnity demanded would be five thousand millions. And, would not we feel the burden if we had to pay our share of that into the coffers of Germany ? Then the people would say of the men now in charge of our affairs that they did not consider the best interests of the Dominion, or of the empire, or they would have sent to the motherland without delay sufficient monev to show, at least, that they were ready and willing to assist her in time of emergency.
Increased knowledge and practice, with a liberal expenditure of money, are perfecting day by day the navies of the world. Well may we say: When will this conflict cease? The nations are vieing with one another to see which will build the best boats and build them in the shortest space of time. The fighting, so far as England is concerned, will be done in the

North Sea. If you follow up what England has been doing with her battleships during the past few months, you will see that she is gradually gathering around her shores in the North sea the best battleships she has. In addition to that, she is protecting her shores to the utmost extent and making all preparation for the war that is likely to take place.
The admiralty made a definite and distinct demand on the people who were represented at this colonial conference, that the best way to assist Great Britain was to keep her navy a unit instead of in separate squadrons as suggested by this Bill. And though the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) may think that he did a noble and a good thing in bringing in this measure, yet, if he will take into consideration the contributions of Australia, New Zealand, and other colonies which have been giving to Great Britain in large proportions to their population, and if he will compare the Dreadnoughts of New Zealand, and the fleet unit of Australia, with the navy that he proposes by this Bill to build in this country, he cannot but see that his navy is not to be compared with the splendid fighting fleet that these other governments are ready and willing to give.
There i3 no question about it, when you consider the means of protecting the British merchant marine, the only way at present, as the members of the admiralty will tell you, is to send a battleship alongside a number of merchantmen to carefully guard them and protect them. So far as our little ships are concerned, they would be no manner of use whatever. On reading the reports of these various conferences, we cannot but feel that the men who represented us were not ready or willing to do even a reasonable amount for the assistance of Great Britain in time of war. Here is the one outstanding fact; the aim in naval warfare is to attain command of the sea; the power that attains this control can attack its enemy where and when it pleases. England has had command of the sea for generations. Fifty years ago her commerce went into every port. At that time, Britain had command of the commerce of the world. To-day, France, Germany, the United States and Russia are vieing with one another to take away that commerce from Great Britain-as they have a perfect right to do. But, we must recognize this fact that it is our duty, as far as British commerce is concerned to assist and protect it to best of our ability. How is command of the sea to be won? Not with such a fleet as is proposed by the government, but simply by the possession of a navy stronger than your opponents. Courage is necessary, and a careful study of the enemy's resources, their naval methods and intentions. An opposing navy could not commit a Mr. ARMSTRONG.
more serious mistake than to detach a squadron with the object of reducing some outlying fleet. She would spoil her concentration, and you would spoil yours if you attempted to follow.
The government say that we must give money and men for the building of a Canadian navy. What have they been doing during the past few years?-spending over a million dollars per annum for the purpose of bringing people to our shores to develop our resources. Would it not be wise to continue this instead of taking money to bring men here for the purpose of assisting in building a navy. The men engaged in the development of these resources, who would otherwise be engaged in the useless defence of our country, would earn sufficient to give a large annual grant to Great Britain, if that were thought advisable. But, I do not believe in an annual grant to Great Britain, and I do not believe we will be called upon to duplicate the two battleships that have been proposed by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition in his splendid resolution. Let us leave the naval question for the present to the powers which have to keep up their navies. Great Britain has the men and we have the money to help her to increase her navy. If we have a navy we have to consider that it means an ever-increasing annual expenditure until that expenditure reaches the sum of $50,000,000 per year. Great Britain will spend on her navy in 1910 $175,000,000. That is $480,000 for every single day of the 365 days in the year. In adition to that she is maintaining her great army at a cost of $430,000 per day. There are $900,000 taken out of the treasury of Great Britain and spent every day for keeping up her army and navy in order that she may protect herself, her colonies and dependencies to which Canada is not contributing one dollar. In addition to that she 3pends $3,000,000 per annum for her consular service to which we do not contribute a dollar. The South African war cost England $1,000,000,000. That, at interest, represents a payment by the British people of $30,000,000 per annum. It is true that Germany, ten years ago, brought in a measure' whereby she set aside $1,000,000,000 for the purpose of building her navy. Since that time she has appropriated $500,000,000 for the same purpose. During this present year she has set aside $105,000,000 for the purpose of building ships, and if you will investigate the German reports, and the German books which tell you of the position of Germany at the present time you cannot but feel that as far as Great Britain is concerned she is not in the position to build these large battleships of the Dreadnought class with the rapidity with which Germany is building them at the present time.

Germany made her plans years ago to construct her dockyards sufficiently large to hold the Dreadnoughts that she is turning out at such a rapid rate. In England's Navy League Annual you will find such facts as these: By the year 1914 Germany, at the present rate of speed will have one ship of the Dreadnought class more than Great Britain will have. You will also see the different firms in Germany which are manufacturing ships of the Dreadnought class and the rapidity with which they are manufacturing these ships. You cannot come to any other conclusion than that which I have indicated with the enormous amount of money that she is expending. Fifty years ago Germany only had $18,000,000 of a debt while to-day she has a debt of $1,000,000,000. Last year she expended $83,000,000 on her navy, and this year she is expending $105,000,000. From year to year, the expenditure has grown until on her army and navy she is expending $224,000,000 this year, or double what the expenditure was in 1900. We know it to be a fact that she has one million men in line, and that she can call upon 4,000,000 more who are fully prepared to fight upon land. We know that she has spent enormous amounts of money in addition to those I have mentioned in preparing her canals and rivers for just such large ships as those of the Dreadnought class. Not only that, but Germany's population is increasing at about the rate of
1,000,000 souls per annum, and her total population ,to-day is 65,000,000 on a land area less than that of the province of Ontario. There is no place for these people to go unless, to some of the colonies owned and controlled by other nations. I do not wish to say one word against the German people as a people. I believe they are a thrifty progressive people, and I sincerely hope that the government, may take steps to bring about better trade relations with Germany, and that they will put a sufficient amount in the estimates to provide for trade representatives who will try and increase our trade with that land. Our government have taken a step in the right direction in the late treaty arrangements, but we are not in as favourable a position in the German markets as we were in 1896. Great Britain's population, in the British Isles, only amounts to 43,000,000 people, and with her limited resources she is spending at the present time $222,000,000 on her army and navy. I have just been handed a copy of to-day's Toronto ' Globe,' in which the following statement appears:
Gathering her Soldiers-Germany ordering her scattered Sons Home-All Unnaturalized Germans in United States receiving Instructions to report for Military Physicm examination-An Order never before issued.
141J
(Special despatch to the ' Globe.')
Dallas, Texas, Feb. 28.-Whether or not she is preparing for war with Great Britain, Germany is serving notice on all her available citizens in the United States to report for military physical examination, to decide if they are still fit for military duty. In view of the fact that this order has never before been issued, and considering the loud talk of war between the countries, this development is full of significance, and shows that Germany is getting all her forces lined up in case a conflict comes. Nearly two hundred Germans of Dallas and Fort Worth who failed to serve their allotted time in the German army have been called upon to submit to physical examinations. Unnaturalized Germans in Texas have been ordered to report to the German Consul at Galveston, where transportation to the fatherland will be supplied.
That is an article which appears in the Toronto ' Globe ' and one which is worthy of consideration. It bears out to some extent the position that the opposition are . taking on this important question. If we are going to assist Great Britain in her wars, now is the time to act. Do not let us wait until we have expended tens of millions of dollars on a useless tin-pot navy, but let us place at once at the disposal of Great Britain a sum sufficient for two Dreadnoughts, and we will be doing something worthy of our country and worthy of the name of patriotic sons of England. We were told by the Minister of Militia, and by other hon. gentlemen oppo site, that a contribution of two Dreadnoughts would mean $25,000,000, but the fact is that the official returns disclose that the largest battleship built in the United States has not cost them $8,000,000 (this estimate did not include guns), and of all the Dreadnoughts turned out of the British dockyards not a single one has exceeded a cost of $8,800,000. Last year the United States spent $219,000,000 on its army and navy, and this year they have given a proof of their anxiety for international peace in reducing that expenditure by $60,000,000. Look at what the countries of the world are doing in naval construction to day, and you will find that not a single one of them is building cruisers of the type which this Bill proposes for their protection. In 1904 Great Britain put out of service 155 ships, and I have no doubt that if we continue to purchase second-hand vessels we will have among our fleet a number of those discarded from the British navy. The control and management of the British navy is under the direction of the Lords of Admiralty, and surely the sea lords should know whether it would be better that we should have a unit of the British fleet or a separate squadron. Practically the first word of the British admiralty to the gen tlemen attending the British conference

was that they would prefer a naval unit I submit, Sir, that the proposition of the leader of the opposition now before the House renders the most effective aid to the motherland at the least cost to our people. When war is declared is not the time for the colonies to help Britain; help must come in advance to be of any use. The Prime Minister has told us that if Great Britain were at war, he would go up and down this country to arouse the people to a sense of their duty, but, Sir, when the smoke of battle is seen and death-dealing missiles are hurtling through the air and Britain calls us to her aid, are we to say Please give us time to think, we have not yet decided whether the war is just or not? Can any one imagine a more humiliating position for a nation such as Canada to be placed in? We are told by the Prime Minister that when the beacon fires are lighted on the hills, Canada would come to the aid of the empire. Yes, but when the beacon fires are lighted on the hills, the war will be on and there will be no time for tire right hon. gentleman to go up and down the country urging assistance. It is our duty to declare that we shall stand by Great Britain always for the sake of the empire, and not when the Governor in Council thinks it fitting that we should do so. The hon. member for Huron (Mr. McLean) tells us that he would investigate whether a war was just or not before sending the fleet, but I can tell him that if the British fleet is defeated on the high seas, Canada will be defeated that same hour. The first few hours of a naval battle decide who shall have command of the seas. The decisive part of the war between Japan and Russia lasted forty minutes, and the taking of Santiago harbour by the United States in the war with Spain took less time than that. Dreadnoughts, and Dreadnoughts alone, will count in the wars of the future. What inducement is there for a young man to enter the Canadian naval service, when he knows that the height of his ambition is limited to command a cruiser that dare not go to war, and which if she went to war would be of no service. It is an insult to the intelligence of our people for the gov; ernment to declare that this navy would only cost $3,000,000 a year, when every one knows that even for such a navy as they propose, it will cost at least eight or ten million dollars ner annum. Does not everything done by the government in this connection, lead us to the inquiry as to whether this is another Grand Trunk Pacific humbug, or another Public Works Department job, or an example of how this business government conducts public affairs? I have tried to place before the government what would be necessary should we attempt to build a navy in the Dominion. I have pointed out that we need a new Welland canal, a new Soo canal, a new Georgian Mr. ARMSTRONG
Bay canal, the Hudson Bay railway, the Hudson straits lighted, and numerous railways and public works in different parts of our country. Last year the government told us that they had to cut down the estimates to the extent of eight or nine million dollars for the want of money, but to-day, just a year after, they appear to have money to bum on a useless navy. Let me point out also that the English navy is a long service navy. Boys enter at Greenwich between 13 years of age and 15, the marines enter between 17 and 23 years of age, and they serve for 12 years. Where are the Canadian boys who are going to train for 12 years in the hope of some day attaining the command of such cruisers as we propose to build? It has been my privilege to have gone through the Greenwich Naval School, and while I have every confidence in the patriotism of the young men of Canada, I do not believe that they are ready to undergo such a training as the boys undergo there, when their only ambition can possibly be such promotion as this proposed navy can afford. Great Britain does not build battleships for coast defence; for that purpose she uses the ships which cannot accompany the fleet, and the pay and salaries in Great Britain are only about one-half of what they would be in Canada. Suppose, for example, such a navy as that which the government proposes were present at the demonstration in the North sea last year, or suppose our little navy should be invited to American waters, how humiliating it would be for the people of Canada to have to admit that they own them. Last year Great Britain sent to the scrap heap 155 vessels of all descriptions. Her age limit for battleships is 25 years, for cruisers 20 years, for destroyers 12 years, so you can readily see that if we build a navy we must continue to build, and pay, pay, pay. This government admits that the construction of the ships will cost us 35 per cent more in Canada than if they were built in England. If the two Dreadnoughts will cost $25,000,000, as the Minister of War says they are likely to, a saving of 35 per cent on that amount would mean $8,750,000 to the people of Canada. If the total cost of two Dreadnoughts would not exceed $20,000,000, which is the proper estimate, then we would save $7,000,000 by having them built in Great Britain^ because the 35 per cent is the difference between $20,000,000 and $27,000,000. Hon. gentlemen opposite talk about giving a preference to Great Britain in our markets and about contributing to her maintenance in so doing. Why not give her a preference by having two battleships built in Great Britain, as proposed by the leader of the opposition, when they can be built there so much better and at. so much less cost? Australia and New Zealand are having their ships built in Great Britain.

Great Britain is the greatest colonizing nation the world has ever known. Germany has tried it, France has tried it, Russia has tried it, Italy has tried it, the United States has tried it, and they have made a complete failure of it. Everybody knows the constitutional principles that govern this country. The King is Commander-in-Chief, here as well as in England, and here this parliament exercises the prerogative as parliament exercises it in England. The King can dissolve this parliament; he is practically the only man who can. Canada is either a part of the British empire or it is not; but this government are driving a wedge between Canada and the motherland by proposing to build an independent navy. [DOT]
All Canadians have hoped that war was a thing of the past, and that as the years went by war would cease. We look at the militarism in force to-day in the nations of Europe, where men in uniform parade the streets and ships of war are constantly in evidence. These nations are burdened with debts and responsibilities that - should warn us against undertaking any such burdens. The nations of the world deplore the state they are in and are seeking means to get away from it. Witness the various naval conferences that have taken place and the means that have been used to maintain peace in different parts of the world. These recognize the futility and needlessness of the barbarous spirit that forces them on. We should be glad that we are privileged to live .in a land of peace, and we should welcome some universal congress of the nations to put a stop to this insane competition for armaments. Why should we, in the light of the twentieth century, when all are talking of the days when war shall be no more, deliberately and voluntarily assume that which other nations are trying to get away from? We like to believe, and there are many signs which show, that mere might is not the only way to conquer. Nations formerly carried on their wars with swords and spears. Now the weapons that are being used, and that should be used, are brains, tariffs and treaties. Building a navy is the first step in the opposite direction. The old-world powers are compelled to keep up their present armies and navies. Why should we attempt to imitate them? The only true position for ns to take is to assist in keeping one central navy, and not to build a separate and independent navy, as proposed by this government. If we follow the government's plan we will add to our expenditures without subtracting from Great Britain's expenditures. Thus far Great Britain has carried us, and in this undertaking we would not be helping her or yet be helping ourselves. It is
recognized that the central imperial navy must be maintained at adequate strength. The question therefore, is, who is going to pay for maintaining it up to the proper standard? The people of Great Britain must do it if we do not assist them. New Zealand says: 'We will give a Dread' nought, and thereby deduct $10,000,000! from the amount of money which the taxpayers of Great Britain will have to ex

pend'. Australia and the other colonies-and dependencies of Great Britain have been saying the same thing. Every dollar they give in the form of a direct grant means a dollar less from the pockets of the English taxpayers, while this government's proposition will not add to the strength of Britain's navy nor deduct a penny from the burden of the British taxpayer. The government of Canada says: 'We will build a little navy of our own. That little navy will be under the control of parliament, and we will not send it to assist Great Britain unless we choose. We will add $17,000,000 to the expenditure and debt of Canada, and place an everlasting burden of annual expenditure on the people of this country.' But the government are unable to show that this expenditure will mean a dollar less of necessary expenditure on the part of the British taxpayer to keep up the imperial navy. What one navy introduces to-day other navies strive to get. Never in the history of the world did false prophets or quacks have better opportunities than they have in this age, and this government can furnish more false prophets and quacks to the square inch, particularly in regard to this question, than any that ever existed before. We can count up an enemy's ships, and calculate the number she will put into line, but we cannot forecast -the ability of her commanders. Who expected Russia to produce a Suvoroff, or Corsica a Napoleon Bonaparte, or Austria a Teget-thoff or Japan a Togo? If we study history, we will thank God- that we have never had a navy to send to sea, and be more than glad if we never will. You may paint a tiger's face on a shield as the Chinese do, but you will need more than the craft if you propose to accomplish anything in war. We cannot mimic or deceive the nations in regard to our naval strength. The world to-day is alive to our military and naval strength, and it is impossible to disguise it. Sea-borne commerce must be defended* and Great Britain's statesmen say that the best way to defend it is by a united navy. There is the convoy method where groups of merchant ships can be escorted by a man-of war, and it is the proper method. What kind of an escort would we give with our puny cruisers and torpedo boats? The ob-

jeet of cruisers is to observe an enemy's force and strength, and return and communicate whatever information they have obtained to the officers waiting. Fighting would be quite outside of their duties. In a cruiser high speed and fuel endurance are necessary, more necessary than ability to fight. We must remain masters of our destinies and not slaves. If we become slaves to war tactics, our energies will become divided. We need all the force and energy we have to develop our resources. Local defence of its very nature must be repeated at many points to be of any service. The enemy will choose the point of attack and the time of attack.
Before we decide on a navy for Canada, let us ask the military class and the working class, the farmer and the artisan, the capitalist and the miner, those who live inland and those who live on our coasts, whether they want for ever to pay, pay, pay. The government has no mandate from the people to force this measure through the House. The only hope for Canada if she embarks on navy building is to set her teeth, build and maintain, and pay, pay, pay. If we are to build and maintain a navy, all parts of our country and all sections of our people must cling together in a manly, patriotic spirit and stand true to our country and to our flag. Let one flag, one fleet, one throne be our motto.
Look at the humiliating spectacle that we are presenting to the world. Canada ready to assert her independence. She will not go to war without the consent of parliament. Are we not drifting towards independence at a rapid rate?
Picture, if you will, Gireat Britain, with its back to the wall, fighting the foe, sending over a request for Canada to come to tier assistance, and the Prime Minister of Canada and his cabinet discussing the merits of the British case and calling parliament together to hear all sides of the question before determining whether we should go to the assistance of the mother country or not.
There is no danger of European nations sending their battleships to Canada until they have defeated the British fleet at home. They would weaken their unit and serve no end. While Great Britain holds command of the sea there is no fear of a foreign foe attacking Canada. Where they would strike would be at. the heart and not at the extremities. Canada's ships, as proposed, will never be called to battle, and after the battle, should Britain's power be supreme, they will not be needed. Should, on the other hand, Britain's power be lost, they will either be sunk or captured.

In closing, let me say to this government: do to England as you would wish England to do to you. If she is in need of help to-day, and I believe she is, you are denying her that help by introducing this Bill. She has asked you for bread, you are offering a stone. You are taking money that you ought to expend to assist Great Britain in building ships to go to the fighting line, like the ships of New Zealand and Australia, and you are instead squandering that money on a useless navy which will be no protection to either Canada or the empire.
If she has displayed ignorance in making her request in the manner that she has, you must remember that had she exposed her whole wish in this matter it would be the public property of her enemies to-day. Stand bv the good old flag and answer England's call, and depend upon it you will never regret it.
An independent navy, as suggested by this government, involves years of delay. The construction and armament of which means enormous capital expenditure, added to which, it will necessarily follow, the un-keep and renewals of our fleet, in addition to the maintenance of schools and academies.
I have unbounded faith in my king and country, and undieing belief in the empire to which I belong. Let the British navy continue to be the floating bulwark of our land and her parliament out guiding star. The most effective contribution we could make, and one which may never need to be repeated, would be to give to England's navy two Dreadnoughts. Then if you must build a navy, submit the whole question to the Canadian people. I am prepared to assist in maintaining the splendid inheritance received from our forefathers. I love my country, I believe in her, I honour her, I am prepared to work for her, to live for her, and, if needs be, die for her.' In order that her territory may remain intact and her name untarnished.

Mr. Speaker, this already long debate of the very important question of the creation of the Canadian navy has, in my opinion, elicited two facts-the wisdom of the measure now before the Chair and the illogical position of the hon. gentlemen who oppose it. The opponents of this measure are divided into two classes- those who are in favour of giving tribute- or, perhaps, I should not use that expression, but let us say, making a contribution -to the British admiralty, and those who

444fi
are in favour of doing nothing at all. The most illogical feature of those who oppose this measure lies, of course, in the fact that, having voted and spoken in favour of the policy expressed in the resolution of the 29th of March last, they now oppose it. The leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden), when this resolution was before the House, took a certain position; to-day, he adopts a different policy altogether. I shall have to quote some parts of the speeches of hon. members opposite, but I shall endeavour to make my quotations as brief as possible, as many of them have been used by other hon. members. Still, in order to make my own argument complete, I think I should be allowed to make a few brief quotations. Here is what the leader of the opposition said when he was addressing the House on the resolution of the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) as reported at page 3517 of ' Hansard ':
In so far as my right hon. friend the Prime Minister to-day outlined the lines of naval defence of this country I am entirely at one with him. I am entirely of opinion, in the first place, that the proper line upon which we should proceed in that regard is the line of having a Canadian naval force of our own. 1 entirely believe in that. The other experiment has been tried as between Australia and the mother country and it has not worked satisfactorily in any respect. In Great Britain the contribution has perhaps been regarded as rather unsatisfactory.
Then, at page 3518:
So, I am at one with the Prime Minister as far as this is concerned. I am at one with him in this respect also that I think that an expenditure of money designed for that purpose ought, in the main at least, to be under the control of our own parliament and that by making an appropriation of that kind and attending to the defence of our own coasts, by co-operation and co-ordination with the imperial naval forces, we would be rendering a real service in defence of the empire and we would be doing our duty not only to Canada but to the empire as a whole.
The leader of the opposition, since that day, has seen fit to change his policy three times. The first policy was on March 29, 1909-rapid construction of a Canadian naval service according to the recommendation of the admiralty; no contribution in money. The second policy appeared on January 12, 1910: Rapid and prudent construction of a Canadian navy, plus a contribution in money to the value of one Dreadnought. Third policy, February 3, 1910:	No Canadian navy: immediate contribution in money to the value of two Dreadnoughts.
Now, Sir, what is the reason of these changes? Everybody knows that the leader of the opposition is a statesman, a very eminent lawyer, able to grasp every question which comes before him, able to analyse a question from all sides. Who can comprehend the reason why he has seen fit, within one year, to change his policy three times?-unless it be that the thumbsrew and the rack_ so much spoken of by the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) have been applied to the leader of the opposition by his own followers. I cannot see any other reason for it. The leader of the opposition has seen fit to increase the tribute he wants this country to pay to the mother country in proportion to the decrease of the German scare. On the 29th of March last, when we discussed the resolution of the hon. member for North Toronto, the German peril cry was launched in England and soon reached this country. Some of us who had not studied the question naturally felt obliged to pause, fearing there might be something in it. At that time, the leader of the opposition was in favour simply of a Canadian navy. But after the thing had been discussed, and when it was found out in England, during the elections, that this was simply an election cry, when the people who govern England, the Prime Minister and some other statesmen said it was simply raised for election purposes, the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) wanted to contribute immediately one Dreadnought. But after the elections were over, when the German scare was found out to amount to nothing, the leader of the opposition declared that he did not want a Canadian navy, but that he did want this country t6 contribute $25,000,000 to the treasury of the admiralty. Well, Sir, I desire to address particularly those gentlemen on the other side of the House who think that a direct contribution is the policy that should be adopted by this country. I wish to quote the admirable argument of the hon. member for North Toronto when he discussed his resolution of the 29th of March last.
