Would they say that we must not protect ourselves now that England has withdrawn her Pacific squadron, and her North Atlantic squadron from our waters, and now that the last of the English troops has departed from Montreal, Quebec, Halifax and Esquimalt, for the mother country. Will they tell them that what was decided at the various conferences was unwise, derisoire, disloyal and unconstitutional? Will they go against the statement made to the House of Commons, by Mr. Asquith on the 29th August, 1909, which is resumed as follows as far as Canada is concerned:
As regards Canada, it was considered that her double sea-boards rendered the provision of the fleet unit of the same kind unsuitable for the present. It was prepared, according to the amount of money, that might be available, that Canada should make a start with cruisers of the ' Bristol ' type and destroyers of the improved river class-a part to be stationed on the Atlantic sea-board and a part on the Pacific.
Will they say that we will not help England in case of danger? Will they say that we don't need the protection of England? Will they say that we must not vote a penny for the defence of Canada? Will they say
to the other dominions and colonies: Do what it pleases you to do, we will not contribute in any shape or form? Will they say our trade with Great Britain and ten or fifteen other British countries, our trade with more than forty or fifty foreign countries need no protection? No, Sir, we know them too well; we all know they would not dare speak such a language. The hon. member for Jacques Cartier has pretended that on this side of the House there were some grinding of the teeth; the hon. member for North Toronto has discovered a composing room, a rack, a thumb-screw and other forms and instruments of torture. These gentlemen must have had terrible nightmares, and it is no wonder. They are fighting so much between themselves that they have lost their heads and all control over their nerves and imagination. The hon. member for Jacques Cartier must be deaf and insensible if he does not hear the grinding of teeth his policy has aroused in his party against the province of Quebec and himself whose sentiments, fortunately, the hon. gentleman does not reflect on that question. He must be insensible if he does not feel the ferocious bites of his warm friends of yesterday and of the last elections; his leaders, the hon. member for North Toronto, the hon. member for Victoria and Haliburton, and last but not least, the hon. member for Frontenac. I am sorry that the hon. member for Jacques Cartier has belittled that national and patriotic question to a paltry party question. Have you heard him accuse his leader of lack of courtesy towards him, and the member for North Toronto, of having failed to keep his word towards him? But, Sir, is it a real fight between the members at your left or a sham battle? It looks as if it is a case where they all agree to disagree -for party purposes. They are preparing, sharpening their favourite weapon, the double-faced policy. But the people have not been fooled in the past and will not be this time either. The people of Quebec will never consent to play that isolation game. What the people of this country expect from us and want us to do is that: Having been chosen- and elected as members of this parliament for its legal term, we shall govern and legislate for the people; having taken the oath, that oath we shall keep; we shall faithfully do our duty to the full measure, without feebleness of faltering; we shall be faithful to the King and to the constitution of our country; that constitution we shall not disobey, but shall preserve intact and sacred; we shall not sacrifice the slightest parcel of our autonomy to jingoism or partisanship; whatever may be the expenditure for the naval defence, we shall spend the money, and the whole of the money in Canada for Canada. Some people pretend that by building a Canadian navy we are helping to break the

bond that ties us so closely to the mothei country. This proposition ,1 cannot entertain for one moment. We shall uphold, and very highly, the dignity of our nation. We shall enjoy to the limit the full liberty of self-government, and we will not allow any one to interfere in our domestic affairs.
Let Canada build her own navy with her own money; let Canada train her own men on her own ships.- In 1775, in 1812, in 1854, in 1865, in 1899, during the African war, and elsewhere, it was our trained men who added lustre to the Canadian name and advanced our progressive march toward nationhood. Canada in making a start with a navy does not intend to enter into any naval competition, but to bear her share in the great work of maintaining the prestige of the Canadian and British names. By making safer her commercial routes, Canada is thus adding to her commercial renown. Canada with a navy, commands more respect as a nation in international relations. Canada's name has become great and respected because of our ties with the British empire, whose grandeur and prestige we are in duty bound to uphold and increase if possible. Let Canada not break those ties., but let her be more and more worthy and proud of her position within the empire.

Mr. Speaker, I desire to trespass for a short time on the attention of the House while I offer a few observations on this important question, in order that there may be no uncertainty in the minds of my constituents as to the position I desire to take on this question, and no uncertainty as to the motives which impel me to take that position. I agree with the hon. gentleman who has just resumed his seat that few questions have occupied the attention of the House which have been fraught with graver results to Canada and her future and which have created greater diversity of opinion than this naval question. I congratulate the hon. member for Laval (Mr. Wilson) upon his very fair presentation of the government's position. He made a patriotic speech, recognizing the plain and manifest duty of Canada to the empire under existing circumstances, and I think it would be well if some of his colleagues from the province of Quebec would follow in his footsteps.
In the discussion of this question it is quite natural that the future of Canada should be canvassed by those who take part in it. What is to be that future? Is Canada to remain an integral part of the British empire or is it destined to become independent and possibly annexed to the United States? If Canada is to remain an integral part of the em-Mr. C. A. WILSON.
pire, what is the only reasonable logical position for her to take, and what is her plain manifest duty at the present juncture? Whatever sentiment there might have been in favour of independence with possible annexation to the United States prior to 1891, was wiped out in that memorable campaign in which that distinguished and respected Conservative leader, the late Sir John Macdonald, sacrificed his life for the maintenance of British connection and institutions, and his rallying cry, 'a British subject I was bom and a British subject I will die,' will go down reverberating through the ages of Canadian history, to steady any waverers in in their allegiance to Great Britain and to strengthen the bonds of Canada and the mother country. And the Hon. Edward Blake, in his famous letter to his electors of West Durham, drove the last nail into the coffin of that traitorous sentiment that then existed. As we are aware, Mr. Blake wrote his constituency prior to 1891, informing them that he was unable to accept the nomination for that constituency because he believed the policy advocated by the leaders of the reform party would ultimately lead to union with the United States, and he further expressed his opinion that the destiny of Canada was irretrievably wrapt up in that of the empire. If Canada is to remain an integral part of the empire what is our duty? There are onlv two courses for us to adopt. One is to do nothing, and thus remain inactive and ' unresponsive to all the demands of duty ana gratitude to the mother country. The other is to do something and thus acknowledge that while we remain a part of the British empire and share in the benefits we must assume .some of the duties, burdens and responsibilities of that relationship.
I have sufficient confidence in the patriotism and sense of justice of the Canadian people to believe that an overwhelming majority are in favour of this House making substantial sacrifices for the benefit of the empire, and the only question on which there should be any possible difference is as to the extent and character of that assistance.
I wrote to a great many of my constituents of both political parties to ascertain their views upon this question, and after a careful perusal of the replies I received, I am at a loss to know what a majority really do want. A very small number desire no expense whatever incurred. A very important and influential body of public opinion desire a cash contribution or a contribution of Dreadnoughts. And a very important and influential body of public opinion desire the construction and organization of a Canadian navy.
This shows that public opinion is still in

a fluid condition, that it has not yet become crystallized; and before any definite permanent policy be entered upon, before this House should lay out a permanent policy, time should be given to the people to canvass the situation more fully.
For reasons some of which have been advanced in this House already, I am unalterably opposed to a cash contribution or even a contribution of Dreadnoughts as a permanent policy of this country. A cash contribution looks too much like paying some one else to do our lighting, and also savours a little of tribute. Canadians are not serfs prepared to contribute their taxes to some sovereign powers beyond our borders, even though it be Great Britain herself. Besides a cash contribution as a permanent policy involves the principle of taxation without representation. which is foreign to our democratic notions of government and is thus an impossible solution..
That there is necessity for making some provision is admitted. The very fact of our making any appropriation at all for this purpose is at once an acknowledgment of the necessity for some provision, and hence, the principle being admitted, the policy being adopted, the extent of our help should be in proportion to the necessity of the case.
if the British navy is being challenged, if the empire is in danger, our assistance must be commensurate with the peril.
Then, the question naturally follows, is there a real emergency in the affairs of the empire?
Is the sword of Damocles suspended over the British navy?
Every student of imperial affairs must acknowledge the gravity of the situation. Germany and England; are at present engaged in a strenuous struggle. A war of construction is now being waged ; a war of destruction may follow. Germany by reason of her geographical position is essentially a military, and not a naval, power. Her inland position without much coast line and without colonial possessions naturally make her an inland power. She possesses the most perfect fighting machine in the world. By intense organization, by her technical education, and toy her highly specialized methods of training^ she has become on land without a peer among the nations of the world. There is no army comparable with hers in efficiency, in numbers and in effective fighting force. It is estimated that she could put in the field upwards of 4,000,000 fighting men.
England on the other hand is essentially a maritime power. Her insular position with vast colonial possessions has peculiarly fitted her for the premier naval position among the nations of the world.
As England at present is supreme on the water, so is Germany supreme on land.
Why are these two great powers not content to allow this equilibrium to be maintained? Why is Germany not content to allow matters to remain in statu quo?
England is content that Germany should maintain her supremacy on land because this is essential to her very existence surrounded as she is with aggressive, watchful and resentful neighbours.
Germany, however, is not content that England should maintain her supremacy on the high seas, although this is essential to the empire's very existence. Germany, with her vaulting ambition, is apparently desirous of being supreme on water as she is now on land. She strives for naval as well as for military supremacy.
If the British fleet demolished the German fleet, Germany would still be immune from successful attack by England's forces by reason of her military strength and power.
But if the German fleet once defeated the British fleet, England's supremacy would be lost-the army of Germany could overrun the country-the British empire would be dismembered, and the rich selfgoverning dominions beyond the seas would in all probability, be the prizes of war- and eventually Canadians would pay dearly for the indifference they have displayed to the empire's interests.
Why then is Germany challenging England's naval supremacy? What is the object and purpose of the great activity? At whom is her great naval programme aimed, if not at England? Her fleet to-day is stronger than the combined fleets of France and Russia. She has nothing to fear from these two powers. What then is her purpose? Germany has a population of 60,000,000 people and is increasing at.the rate of 1,000,000 each year. She must secure colonial outposts for her surplus population to which her subjects may emigrate and continue to live under the German flag and suzerainty. Canada, New Zealand, Australia and South Africa would make rich prizes for any nation to contend for.
Max O'Rell, the famous French lecturer says that France fights for glory; Germany fights for a living, but England fights for trade and peace.
I have heard a number of hon. gentlemen opposite on the floor of this House declare on several occasions that the Monroe doctrine would protect Canada in the last analysis. I say that such a declaration is unworthy of any Canadian. I was pleased to hear the Postmaster General (Mr. Le-mieux) and the hon. member for Sunbury and Queens (Mr. H. H. McLean) resent the imputation that was cast upon Canadian character by some of their colleagues. To entertain the idea that we could look with complacency to a foreign country for protection is revolting to any true British subject, and to rely upon the indefinite and

uncertain policy of a foreign country known as the Monroe doctrine is to lean upon a broken, at any rate an untried reed, and to pace us at the mercy of and under obligation to a foreign country. Such a prospect does not commend itself to the patriotism of any true Canadian. Sir, to state such a proposition is to dismiss it from our minds. The question. I think, must be answered, and the course of this parliament must be determined by the answer to that question: Is there a real emergency in the affairs of the empire? If there is, the insignificant contribution offered by this government is of no assistance in the time of need. Long before the general elections in the old country, British statesmen speaking upon the status of the British navy as compared with foreign navies, raised distress signals. They sounded cries of alarm at Germany's naval activity. During the elections, they attempted to neutralize the effect of their previous statements; but it was too late, the people took them at their word, as that word had been uttered prior to the election excitement. Hon. members opposite offer many authorities to prove that there is no menace at the present time from Germany, no emergency in the affairs of the empire. But of all the authorities that were quoted, the most peculiar and extraordinary was that quoted by the Minister of Militia (Sir Frederick Borden). That hon. gentleman quoted from a speech of the German ambassador who, he said, was speaking in England-I presume making an after-dinner speech-to show the pacific intentions of Germany towards Great Britain. That is the proof the hon. gentleman relied upon -that the German ambassador, speaking in England, told the English people, in an after-dinner speech that Germany's intentions were not hostile and that Germany was not intending to attack England, because of these preparations. As has been stated here, the German people are not the people to hunt ducks with a brass band.
Now, the wisest men in both political parties have conceded the absolute necessity of maintaining Great Britain's naval supremacy. Mr. Gladstone, in 1878, used these words:
The strength of England is not to be found in alliances with great military powers but is to be found henceforth in the efficiency and supremacy of her navy-a navy as powerful as the navies of all Europe.
And Sir Edward Grey, Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs, in June, 1909, said:
The navy is the common security of the whole empire. If it ever fails to be that it will be of no use to discuss any other subjects, and the maintenance of the navy in that position must therefore he the care, not only of us at home, but of the self-governing dominions beyond tbe seas.

At the imperial press conference, one of the colonial press men interviewed Sir Edward Grey, and the result was published in the Evening ' Journal ' of Thursday, January 27, 1910. Sir Edward Grey, upon that occasion, said:
I cannot think that there is a likelihood of war. I cannot bring myself to believe that a great and intelligent and Christian nation like Germany could attack us without provocation -without grave fault on our own side. But I am compelled to admit that the historical fact is that in the course of her imperial expansion, Germany has in our time gone more than half way to meet war with Denmark, with Austria and with Prance, and has within a few weeks practically presented an ultimatum to Russia giving the option of war or silence regarding the annexation by Austria of Bosnia and Herzegovina. We must face the possibility that our turn might come. It is possible, though I cannot think it probable, that if Germany were strong enough on the sea to risk an encounter with our navy the encounter might ensue in spite of ourselves.
If war were to come, and our navy were worsted, it would spell the ruin of the British empire. Germany would not need to land a soldier in England. Our food comes across the seas. We could be starved into absolute submission in a month.
No other great power has to face such a consequence of defeat.
We have two courses open. One, to allow Germany to easily catch up with us in sea power, and take the chance of a quarrel. The other, to try to keep so far ahead of her naval force that no quarrel will occur.
The latter course seems the necessary one. The possibilities of the other are too grave to risk so long as our resources enable us to keep ahead.
I would hardly contradict any one who would say that it is a hundred-to-one chance against our having war with Germany even when Germany has arrived in a position to risk it. And yet I am compelled to feel that even though it be a hundred-to-one shot against war, we must not, if we can help it, take even a single chance when that single chance includes the possibilitv of the ruin of England-the possibility of the end of our thousand years of English story.
And Sir Edward Grey spoke on March 29 in the House of Commons, and is reported in volume 3 of ' Hansard ' of 1909, page 54, as follows:
First of all the House and the country are perfectly right in the view that the situation is grave. A new situation in this country is created by the German programme. Whether that programme is carried out quickly or slowly the fact of its existence makes a new situation. When that programme is completed, Germany, a great country close to our shore will have a fleet of 33 Dreadnoughts. That fleet would be the most powerful which tbe world has ever yet seen. It is true that there is not one of them in commission yet; but it is equally true that the whole programme comprises what I have said, and when completed the new fleet will I be the most powerful fleet which the world

has yet seen. That imposes upon us the necessity, of which we are now at the beginning-except so far as we have Dreadnoughts already-of rebuilding the whole of our fleet. That is what the situation is. What we do not know is the time in which we shall have to do it.
We must he prepared to defend our national existence under the conditions which are imposed upon us in our own generation. I am glad that it is not to us alone that this feeling is confined. I am glad that the colonies, such as New Zealand recognize that their national existence is one with us in this matter.
The friends of the government, including the leader of the House (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) in their speeches have' quoted Lord Charles Beresford as being in favour of local navies for the component parts of the empire. They do not, however, accept his statement that there is a real peril, and that the true policy is one of preparedness on the part of the British navy. I submit that if they accept him as the highest authority on one point, they are bound to accept him on the other. Lord Charles Beresford on January 1, 1910, spoke as follows:
Germans have said that if they intended to attack England it would be without warning. I suggest that Germany would send out her tramps with six-pounders and attack the trade routes-and even a tramp could sink a Mauretania. The pretext is easy-a little difficulty about Holland or Belgium, the Congo, or the TPersian gulf, a diplomatic letter would follow, and what is to stop Germany from striking a blow at night and getting hold of the trade routes? Great Britain has left her arteries undefended.
I say seriously that Germany is deliberately challenging us to make all preparations.

Balfour, leader of the Conservative opposition, speaking on January 4, 1910, said:
He hoped and believed that Germany and Britain may not come into conflict, but said the diplomats of the lesser powers did not share this view. He insisted that Britain was now in a position as regards her navy which she had not been in within the memory of living men. Indeed, her naval superiority on her own seas would be threatened within the near future.
' I don't believe there is going to be war between this country and any great foreign power/ he exclaimed. r Heaven knows I don't desire it. I don't believe it. But please remember that absolutely the only way in which you can secure the peace which you all desire is that you shall be sure of victory if war takes place.'	. .
The empire existed only on sufferance if the navy were not supreme, and he was not content to exist on sufferance.
Now, I purpose quoting a gentleman who has been somewhat assailed in this House, Mr. Robert Blatchford. Mr. Blatchford is
a talented and educated socialist who wrote for the ' Daily Mail ' in London in connection with the German peril. His principles are opposed to a military and naval programme, but in this crisis he subordinates his principles to the welfare and salvation of the empire. In this crisis he was a British subject first and a socialist afterwards. He wrote as follows:
The strongest evidence of Germany's designs against Britain is the German navy. There can be no stronger evidence of any nation's intention to make war than that afforded by wholesale, feverish, and systematic preparations for war.
Now the German preparations are na\;. preparations. Against whom can these preparations be directed if they are not directed against us? Manifestly they are not meant for Russia, nor for I'rance, nor for Amci.,... The magnitude of the preparations points to a prospective struggle with a fleet more powerful than that of Russia or France.
The construction of the German ships prohibits their use in distant seas, against Japan for instance, or the United States. And whereas we have been told in a hundred books and newspapers and pamphlets and speeches that the German navy is meant to wrest from Britain her command of the sea. it would be difficult to find a single German suggestion that the German navy is meant to try conclusions with any power other than Britain. Germany can reach France oi Russia by land. Her fleet is already moro than a match for France or Russia combined Her fleet is built for the North sea, it is exercised in the North sea, it remains in the North Sea.	.
Her ships were built against our ships, the object of the German builders being always to go one better than the British in each type. .	.	. If we do not want to war with
Germany, we must be strong enough to want Germany to cause peace.
Though Germany is a brave, resolute, and mighty enemy, she is not omnipotent, nor is she invulnerable. But she means business-blood and iron business-and all conciliation, subterfuge, and compromise provoke her to contempt and scorn. ...
Germany outs her destinies into the hands of warriors; we leave ours in the hands of politicians. Germany acts; we talk. Words count for nothing in the game of blood and iron. _	.
Arm or surrender; fight for the empire oi loose it. We can choose our alternative; no middle course is open to us.
Now, I submit that when prominent British statesmen on both sides of politics agree in pointing out the gravity of the situation, we as Canadians cannot longer remain indifferent. British statesmen are not extremists, they are not jingoes, they are not alarmists, their language is not violent or exaggerated; their utterances are usually characterized by discretion and moderation, and consequently we should give due weight to their deliberate judgment upon this supreme issue. I think that on the evidence

adduced it must be conceded that the British navy is menaced at the present time toy the German naval programme, and the question naturally suggests itself: Is the Naval Bill introduced by the government commensurate with Canada's duty to the empire? Does' it discharge our plain and full duty to the empire under existing circumstances? In my humble opinion the government has lamentably failed to meet the situation. It is a matter of universal regret that the government has refused to comply with the wishes and plans of the British admiralty as outlined at the recent conference of 1909. The British admiralty are peculiarly fitted and specially adapted to know the wants and needs of the British navy, and they expressed their preferences for certain lines of action, but the Canadian government refused to meet their wishes. In the first place, the British admiralty suggested as an ideal method of assisting the navy, a money contribution, but this was refused. Then they suggested a complete fleet unit which would include a Dreadnought, but this was refused. Then they suggested that this fleet unit should be stationed on the Pacific coast in order to relieve the British men-of-war stationed there, and this was refused. Then they expressed the opinion that the local naval forces, in the event of war, should come under the immediate command of the British admiralty, but this was refused, and made subject to the consent of the Governor in Conucil. The ideal of the British admiralty was that the five component parts of the British empire should each furnish a fleet unit which would, in time of war, come under the control and command of the British admiralty in case of emergency. Canada's danger lies in the defeat of the British navy. Once it is defeated, Canada's contribution of her insignificant defensive force would be of no avail whatever. Canada, in my opinion, should have organized a fleet unit as suggested by the British admiralty, and when the summons to arms was issued, that each fleet unit from the colonies should proceed tu array itself with the British navy and forming a component part thereof dovetail into that great fighting machine. When you compare the fleet units as suggested by the British admiralty with that contemplated by the government's Bill, there is not much difference in the number of ships, nor in the actual maintenance charges. The fleet unit as suggested by the British admiralty consisted of 13 ships, being one armoured cruiser of the ' Indomitable ' class and of the Dreadnought type, three protected cruisers, six destroyers and three submarines, costing $18,500,000, and _ the maintenance charges amounting to .$3,1500,000. The proposed Canadian unit consists of 11 ships, being 4 Bristols, 1 Boadecea and 6 destroyers, costing $11,000,000, and the Mr. S. SHARPE.
annual maintenance charges being $2,500,-
000.	In the matter of initial expense there was only a difference of $7,500,000, and for annual upkeep, a difference of $500,000; But there is a great difference in the effective fighting force of the two units. But the government programme makes no provision for a Dreadnought, and a Dreadnought is the effective fighting machine in modern naval warfare. Superiority in Dreadnoughts will decide the naval supremacy of the future. The British admiralty asked for a complete fleet unit, a living vital fighting force. This government is merely presenting a skeleton without any effective striking power. Hence, I submit there are two fatal defects in the programme of the government which make it impossible for me to support the measure. Although I have in the past expressed myself in favour of the principle of a Canadian navy as a permanent policy, there are two fatal defects in the government programme. One is the absence of a Dreadnought, which would have formed part of the fleet had the government organized a fleet unit; and the other is the presence of a condition that the navy will assist the empire only with the consent of the Governor in Council. Paragraphs 17, 18 and 19 of the Bill are fatal paragraphs, in connection with this measure. Paragraphs 17 and 18 read:
17.	The Governor in Council may place the naval forces or any part thereof, on active service at any time when it appears advisable so to do by reason of an emergency.
18.	In case of an emergency the Governor in Council may place at the disposal of jHi* Majesty, for general service in the royal navy, the naval service or any part thereof, any ships or vessels of the naval service, and the officers and seamen serving in such ships or vessels, or any officers or seamen belonging to the naval service.
And section 19 provides that parliament shall be called for a meeting within fifteen days after the Governor in Council has placed the naval service on active service. These clauses, in my opinion, destroy the whole effect and purpose of the government's Bill. A few men in the cabinet could withhold the consent of the Governor in Council for a considerable time, and in the meantime the British navy might be annihilated. These clauses may become in effect and substance a declaration of independence. Should war be declared against the empire, and should this government decide not to allow our so-called navy to participate in the empire's wars, down would come the British flag and up would go the Canadian ensign. I submit that this is tantamount to a declaration of independence. Should our Canadian navy stand aloof from the British navy in time of great national danger? I would like to ask if our so-called navy, when organized

and constructed, is to be ordered up the St. Lawrence and Ottawa rivers to be anchored to parliament hill until this fickle, faltering cabinet shall have come to some compromise decision in reference to its ultimate destiny? Personally, I am in favour of the principle of a Canadian navy as a definite permanent policy.for Canada, but I want an effective fighting force-a complete ' fleet unit,' under the central control of the British admiralty, and not subject to the delays nor to the whims and caprices of a hesitating, halting, vacillating cabinet, which in the past has not displayed any great alacrity in assisting the empire in time of great stress and danger.
The leader of the government in his Toronto speech said that the British navy had a displacement of 2,000,000 tonnage, while Germany had only about 600,000 tons displacement. He, thereby, made* the deduction that the British navy was far superior to the German navy, and attempted to minimize the gravity of the present situation. But I submit that this is not a fair basis of comparison. It is not by tonnage displacement that the efficiency, the effective striking force, of a navy is estimated, but -by the number of its Dreadnoughts. It is not the number of obsolete war vessels (of which all count in the computation of tonnage), but it is the number of Dreadnoughts that will decide the naval supremacy of the future. Germany in 1912 or thereabouts, will have more Dreadnoughts, if their present plans be carried out, than England, and hence by this Dreadnought standard of comparison (the only real standard) England is in danger of losing her supremacy.
Hence the present Bill ignores the vital matters in this titanic struggle, and when Germany and England engage in the inevitable final combat Canada's insignificant contribution, handicapped by conditions that will thwart and defeat its very purpose, will not be able to appear in the imperial firing line doing effective service, (along with New Zealand and Australia), in defence of the empire.
Is this inferior-position not humiliating to every Canadian subject? Contrast the position of Canada with that of our sister colonies-Australia and New Zealand-and is there a Canadian that does not feel deeply humiliated? In comparison with New Zealand and Australia our efforts are feeble, our efforts are unworthy of our people, unworthy of our vast resources, unworthv of our premier position as the richest and most populous self-governing nation in the empire.
But what else could the people of Canada expect? The leader of the government is always eloquent when the occasion requires eloquent in hjs loyalty, and loyal in his eloquence-and if loyal speeches
could win battles Canada alone could furnish ' invincible armadas ' comprising stacks of bound volumes of ' Hansard ' and illustrated editions of the Toronto ' Globe '.
But while we indulge ourselves in the harmless and pleasant occupation of making patriotic speeches, and passing loyal resolutions, our sister nations (New Zealand and Australia) are offering Dreadnoughts and fleet units to the empire.
Humiliation! This is not the first occasion on which the bitter draught has been placed to the lips of Canada by this government. This is not the first time Canada has trailed in the rear of her sister colonies instead of blazing the way. When war was declared in South Africa, and German intervention was feared, where was the leader of the government? Where was Canada when all the other colonies were vieing with each other in rushing troops to the scene of hostilities? The right hon. leader of the government was giving an interview to the Toronto ' Globe ' of October 4, 1899, as follows:
The Premier's Statement.-Government has
made no offer of Troops to the Imperial
Authorities.
There is no menace to Canada, and although we may be willing to contribute troops, I do not see how we can do so. Then, again, how could we do so without parliament granting us the money? We simply could not do anything. In other words, we should have to summon parliament. . . . And so it is that we have not offered a Canadian contingent to the home authorities. The Militia Department duly transmitted individual offers to the imperial government and the reply from the war office, as published in Saturday's ' Globe,' shows their attitude on the question. As to Canada's furnishing a contingent, the government has not discussed the question, for the reasons which I have stated, reasons which I think must easily be understood by every one who understands the constitutional law on the question.
Does that memorable interview display any enthusiasm for imperial interests?
What happened is familiar to all:	The
public clamoured for action, the press was loaded with protests, the wave of patriotism throughout Canada became irresistible and would have swept the government, out of existence had it not yielded to the popular demands. Not one, but many Canadian contingents were sent to distinguish themselves along 'with the Australian and New Zealand contingents, and their life's blood has left indelible- stains upon the veldts of South Africa and brought imperishable fame Upon Canadian valour. Ab though all Canada knows full well that the leader of the government resisted to the utmost the sending of the Canadian contingents to assist the empire in the Boer war, and not a man would have been sent, nor a dollar spent if

he had had his way, yet when the wax was over and victory had been won by the valour of the imperial troops, the right hon. leader and his supporters took all the credit to themselves-they presented themselves with all sorts of bouquets, waved the old flag and sang the national anthem over and over again. They have been turning handsprings in their paroxisms of loyalty ever since, little surmising that their outbursts of loyalty would soon again be put to the test. The government is now being tested-they are standing under the measuring rod. Are they measuring up to the full stature of their professions? It is for the Canadian people to say after a perusal of this proposed Naval Bill.
^Now, we come to the question of what Canada's duty is at the present time. If the supremacy of the British navy is being challenged, and I believe it is, if the emergency be pressing, urgent and compelling, and I believe it is, then this House should act and act promptly, definitely and decisively. It is Canada's duty to order, not one, two or three Dreadnoughts, but a sufficient number of Dreadnoughts to meet the emergency. We should order Dreadnoughts according to the extent of the peril, according to the magnitude of the danger to be apprehended, according to the exigencies of the case. These Dreadnoughts should be manned with British men and officers until Canadians can be trained for the service-all at the expense of Canada. Then the question of Canada's permanent policy should be left to the people. Having thus, in part, atoned for our past neglect, and having, in part, liquidated our obligation of long standing, we could then consider with due deliberation and with due regard to our constitutional obligations to the electors who have sent us here, the permanent policy which this country should adopt in regard to the construction, organization and maintenance of a Canadian navy service. Then we would have time to consider and adjust all imperial questions relating to the navy and its relationship to the empire-the question of the control and final command of the navy in time of war and what voice Canada is to have in deciding imperial questions. The peonle of Canada have a right to be heard before this permanent policy is decided unon. We have no mandate from the electors. The public have a right to be heard for many substantial reasons. The government, it is true, says that this question has been before the people since 1902. I challenge the truth of that statement, but even if it be true, that this question has been before the people since 1902, what has the policy of the government been since 1902? Absolutely opposed to the construction of the Canadian navy or to any contribution towards imperial defence. If the question has been Mr. S. SHARPE
before the people in the elections of 1904 and 1908, they have pronounced against the construction of a Canadian navy or any contribution to imperial defence, and now the government, by the present Bill, is flying in the face of the result of these two general elections. But, everybody knows that this is. a. new policy and that it has never been discussed in any general elec* tion. The question is far reaching and involves large and permament obligations upon the country. Important public bodies have requested that the question should be submitted to the people before the government inaugurates a new policy upon which the people have not had an opportunity of pronouncing. I refer to the Dominion Grange and the Manitoba Grain Growers' Association, and I may add that the ' Weekly Sun ' and other piominent papers that represent a very large sentiment that exists throughout the province of Quebec and in other provinces demand that the question should be submitted to the people before any definite permanent policy is inaugurated. Whenever a new and important policy is being framed it is usual, and the constitutional practice is, to appeal to the people or to postpone the inauguration of the policy until after the electors have have had an opportunity to pronounce upon it. As 1 stated a short time ago, I am in favour of the principle, as a permanent policy for Canada, of the construction, organization and maintenance of a Canadian navy. That, to my mind, is the only proper solution of this important question. True. I believe that the prevailing sentiment of Canada is against the construction of a Canadian navy and in favour of a contribution by Canada of cash or Dreadnoughts to the empire. Does any one imagine that a cash contribution or a contribution of Dreadnoughts will discharge Canada from further contributions and relieve her from all future obligations? Not at all. The British navy must be maintained and Canada must continue, in some form, its assistance to imperial defence. Canada must adopt some definite permanent policy of continuous assistance. And, Sir, in my opinion, as a permanent policy, either a cash or a Dreadnought contribution is an impossible solution. The government has, subject to the approval of the people, if it were submitted to the people-adopted in my view, the correct principle, of constructing, organizing and maintaining a Canadian navy, thereby exploiting and utilizing our vast natural resources in building up a great industry in Canada. But while adopting the correct principle, the government has destroyed the objects and purposes of a Canadian navy - by not makin0, it a complete fleet unit and by annexing an impossible condition to its service under the control of the British ad-

miralty, namely: that it cannot go to war without the consent of the Governor General in Council. If the government of Canada intend doing anything tovrards assisting the empire in its time of stress and need, she should do something generous, and she should do that something promptly. To accomplish that it is necessary to organize a complete fleet unit with a Dreadnought at the head and not. subjected to any bonds or chains in the form of onerous conditions. Had the government taken this course it would have commanded the respect and support of a large and important body of public opinion.
Let us suppose, Mr. Speaker, that a Conservative government were in power, do you think that that Conservative administration would have brought down such a Bill as this? I do not believe it would. As this Liberal government refuses to recognize Canada's duty to the empire, and has failed to interpret the will of the people in that regard, and as its contribution is not a true index of the heart and feelings of the people of Canada, it may devolve upon the Conservative premiers of the four provinces under Conservative administrations to get together and devise some scheme whereby one or two Dreadnoughts shall be sent to the empire as Canada's contribution. I believe, Mr. Speaker, that it is a great misfortune, not only for Canada, but for the empire, that a Conservative administration has not been in control of the affairs of Canada during the past ten or fifteen years. Had the Conservative party been in power during these momentous times, and particularly during the imperial conferences, I am absolutely satisfied that some satisfactory scheme or plan of imperial federation would have been devised, and put into operation, and I believe that long before this an imperial council representative of all parts of the empire would have been created, and the dream of all true British subjects would have become a reality. This Liberal government in Canada has always applied the /brakes to any such movement, and it has not only refused to assist, but has absolutely discouraged any such plan at every turn, and on every opportunity. When war was declared in South Africa, the government of Canada lagged behind all other *colonial governments, and showed no sympathy with the empire. At the imperial conference of 1907, the leader of the government expressly refused to support a motion, introduced by one of the colonial delegates, which was calculated to unite the emDire into bonds of closer union. The grumbling assent of this government to the imperial conference of 1909, to the military and naval defence committee, and the niggardly policy as outlined in this
Bill all show a lack of enthusiasm for imperial interests.
Now, Sir, in conclusion, I think, that it is the duty of Canada to place an immediate order for Dreadnoughts to form a part of the Canadian navy and to act in co-operation with and as a part of the imperial navy and under the control, in times of danger and emergency, of the British admiralty. We should then postpone the inauguration of any permanent policy until the Canadian people have been heard from, either by means of a referendum or in a general election. In the meantime, speaking for myself, I desire to go on record, as I have done on previous occasions in my own constituency, and in the corridors of the House, where I have expressed myself in favour of the principle of a Canadian navy. I desire to go on record as in favour of the principle of a Canadian navy as the means best calculated to serve the interests of the empire of the future, and best calculated to work out the great destiny of this country. I regret, therefore, that I cannot support this Naval Bill of the government, because of its meagreness, its niggardliness in not providing for a fleet unit as it should have done, and also because of the impossible condition that the government has annexed to its service in the empire's wars, which condition must render it unsatisfactory to every true Canadian who loves British institutions and British liberty, who is conscious of our deep obligations to the mother country, and who believes that universal peace depends on the maintenance of British supremacy, which is now being challenged and jeopardized by England's greatest commercial, military and naval rival.

BOYER (VaUdreuil.) (Translation.) Mr. Speaker, it would be commonplace to undertake to prove that Canada passes through an important national evolution. Everbody feels this and it is admitted by all, but every one does not see the causes. These causes are not very complicated and I will try to place them before the House.
Modern nations should never be isolated, as Ch'na has done in the past to. its detriment. The policy of each of them depends more or less upon the policy of the rival nations, and all are ruled by one great law, the international law.
Well, let us see what has given rise to this evolution of this sort of crises through which we now pass, and which forces us at this moment, willingly or unwillingly, to come to a decision upon which our future will rest.
A great European nation, Germany seeks domination. She is fatally brought to that, not so much because her citizens love warfare or hazardous adventures, but because

she has a very large population, and is congested in her own territory, so that she must look for other fields and colonies for expansion. Germany must fight an economical war. England is situated in somewhat an analogous position, but on account of her supremacy on the seas, 'she has by this very fact the outlets which the other nation needs.
Many will say, this economic war will not turn into actual war. Let us hope that they are right, but we must admit that appearances do not justify this optimism. On both sides armaments are going on frantically, so much that in both countries the budgets are frightfully surcharged and one of these nations thought proper to say to its colonies, " Look at the sacrifices which I am obliged to make. Will you not help me? "
" We will gladly help you " responded the over-seas dominions, of which Canada is one.
" And how will you do it? "
Firstly by taking on ourselves the defence of opr territory and our shores; secondly by lending you our troops and our ships, if you are attacked.
This is a natural and proper answer, because :
1.	A free nation surrounded by armed nations, must necessarily assume the means of defending herself.
2.	Unless being absolutely blind, a people cannot refuse to defend its own home and civilization, when such are threatened with destruction.
The interest of Canada is twofold, because it is inhabited by two races who spring from the civilization of two great peoples, who for a long time were rivals, but now attached to one another. We have not two metropolises, one Anglo-Saxon, the other French. And let this not be forgotten. The latter would suffer just as much as the former by a war which would hand over the domination to a foreign civilization opposed to the ideas and the traditions which animate both of these two national groups.
We are consequently confronted by the following problem:
1.	Is it necessary that we should defend the territory and the coasts of Canada?
2.	If so, shall we undertake ourselves this country, take charge of it? Is it neces-fence or let Great Britain, our mother saTy to defend our country? The question is answered by itself; but there are some *who hold a different view. But have they ever clearly understood that Canada is one of the greatest countries of the earth, on account of its territory and natural resources; that if it is not parcelled in the future it will be one of the most powerful. Canada holds already almost the foremost rank through its agricultural products and

through the development of its merchant shipping. Its mineral resources are immense. Its forests cover the country from one ocean to the other, and we have on that score reserves of the world.
All over the country there is at present a fever of development. AVealth flows like a wave in the west. The great provinces of the centre stand already amongst the strongest foundations of the world. In a word, everything in our country is so great that we cannot grasp it.
Let us merely glance at a part of our maritime coast. Let us go through that region which extends from Montreal, our commercial metropolis, to the extreme end of the Gulf of St. Lawrence. The river of that name is the grand waterway of our trade, and through its whole length is navigated by hundreds of ships, the imposing transatlantic steamer as well as the humble schooner or the fisherman's boat. AAre first come across a pleasing country of a remarkable beauty and fertility, and further on we find mountainous regions, dark and wooded, but everywhere we behold villages, fields, herds of cattle and industrial establishments 'busy and flourishing, till we come at the entrance of the Gulf, and to the coal fields of Gape Breton; they are immense, and the only ones we find on the Atlantic *coast, even if -we were to travel from one pole to the other. They are situated precisely at the spot where the American continent is nearest the continent of Europe.
It is there that France erected the fort of Louisburg, under the walls of which the fate of the new world was decided.
Looking at these ruins one is struck by the wisdom /of the great engineer who selected this place from which a vessel could go out and offer battle to the enemy coming from the east, between Cape Breton and Newfoundland. While the enemy that might have seized that place, could block the route to Canada and demolish all the plan of defence. That is what happened, as we know, after the capture of Louisburg by General Wolfe. To-day this military position is still most important. The coal fields of Cape Breton had become for modern navy purposes, an inexhaustible and essential defensive post. Who holds it holds doubly the key to Canada on the Atlantic. That fort defends treasures of forests and fisheries which the general of Louis XV. could not imagine. But principally this lengthy north coast, with its aspect so inhospitable, but composed of iron, -white coal and deep ports, cannot pally this lengthy north coast, with its dockyard for steel vessels.
The Pacific coast offers the spectacle of natural wealth almost equal; but it is not necessary for me to go on further with this demonstration. We the owners of this wealth, are completely disarmed on the sea. Around us everybody, all nations are

in arms. In the east we see Japan, immediately to the south, United States, one of the great naval powers of the world in Central America, each republic has its war vessels. In Europe, as we know, some great military nations are congested foi want of colonies.	.
Under these circumstances how long will we remain free asd protected against the ills of war, if we do not defend ourselves? We are too rich a prey not to excite the covetousness of others. If Great Britain were not there, is it not evident that we would inevitably fall under the tutelage of some other great nation that would make us pay very dear for the protection which she would give us, and it would be a great chance if she did not absorb us completely? Of this common sense alone will convince us; it is not even necessary to read the significant comments which are printed every day in the papers of the nations that have their eyes on us.
Is it our duty to defend ourselves as much as we can in our present conditions?. I say yes. It is not surely for lack of citizenship that some Canadians are opposed to the idea of an effort on our part to defend Canada on the sea. They look at the question from another point of view, and they say that our money would be far better utilized in developing our natural resources. They would be right if the world were disarmed.
Unfortunately, our dignity as well as our interest demands that we should leave no stone unturned to accomplish by our own initiative this essential duty.
I say that it is our interest, and where could we find in the history of the world a people who has succeeded in keeping his national life by leaving the care of his defence to other arms, even to those of friends or allies? We cannot find one. In the life of nations as in the life of individuals, interest is the measure of actions; every one looks before all to things which are of personal interest to himself. It is the law of the world; who will not respect it will fall. The present emergency recalls that law, and Great Britain herself who has protected us heretofore is in need of our help, towards maintaining her rank and dignity among the nations.
Besides, the practice of military and naval arts, carries with it certain important and direct advantages. While increasing the strength of the country, the energy and self-reliance of its inhabitants, it helps powerfully, through the exertions it requires, in promoting the progress of the human race. Is it not owing to war, owing to the efforts made in defending a position or directing an attack that many modern discoveries have been effected.
On the other hand, the establishment of a national navy for Canada will bring with it direct substantial benefits. Great dockyards will be provided which will give employment to many hands, while at the same time developing to great extent our resources. A certain number of our young men will receive from year to year instruction and training in the naval schools; the spirit of discipline acquired while on duty will be an education in itself; numerous families of seamen inhabiting our coasts, and whom the dwindling of the coasting trade has impoverished, will see the good old times recur; a trip to our maritime sections enables one to realize the need for such a revival. As we all know, on the coasts of England, France, and Norway, the sons of fishermen on returning home after doing service on the warships, no longer show the spirit of routine, at any rate not to the same degree as formerly; they show a greater openness of mind, they are no longer chary of innovations which make for greater prosperity and happiness. Such influences are of a nature to transform a people by developing their abilities and imparting selfreliance and initiative.
Of course, all these things will of neces- [DOT] sity cost a great deal; and that is the stock argument of our special pleaders. Do you not perceive, say they, that we are disbursing large sums for providing a navy which will never be in a position to hold its ground against those of the great powers. In other words, you are going to provide a mock navy, a tin-pot navy. Under the circumstances we would be better off with no navy at all, and if we are bound to make sacrifices let it be in the shape of a yearly money contribution to the British navy, and let that settle the matter.
Such a plan is entirely without foundation. What I have previously said is sufficient evidence to that effect; but there is more, and much more, that could be said. Canada is not yet a great nation, at any rate in point of population, but that is increasing rapidly. The next census has in stock for us great and pleasant surprises. Twenty years hence, our numbers will greatly exceed twenty millions, and we will actually be a numerous and very wealthy people. Will we be powerful as well? That depends on what steps we decide to take just now. Possibly, we may be a mere human hive without strength or dignity; it might even happen that our national existence would be done away with. A fleet of warships cannot be created in a moment. Several _ years of preparation are necessary to provide fully equipped dockyards, under competent management, with skilled workmen, well trained officers and men.
That is the work to which we are setting ourselves just now. It might have been wiser to start before now, but we were not at liberty to do so. And when all these meausures have been taken, we will be in a position to hold our own among the na-



But does this mean that the French Canadians are disloyal to England, because a certain number do not like the principle of this Bill in which they may perhaps find too pronounced a tendency towards imperialism, while a certain number of others here protest more or less discordantly because of the enormous expenditure the measure will entail. After all, let us frankly admit it; the French Canadian cannot have the /Same reasons as his English speaking fellow citizen to become enthusiastic in this matter, because in his case blood relationship does not exist; nevertheless, his attachment to the British crown is too evident for his loyalty to be one moment doubted; albeit it must be admitted that with him, the favourable appreciation of the naval question comes from a feeling of gratitude and justice.
I might, Mr. Speaker, cite many of my English-speaking fellow-citizens who have taken up either one or the other of the points of view to judge of the merit of the measure that we are at present discussing, and who will never be accused of disloyalty for all that.
I therefore appeal to the spirit of justice of my opponents and I would ask them in future to conduct their plans of attack on other grounds than that of the French nationality. That we have our fanatics, that is true, and they have perfect right to exist, to discuss and to bring forth their theories as the fanatics of the English language, but they are not the less loyal for all that.
One consideration, Mr. Speaker, and this one alone would be sufficient to secure my support to any measure of a nature to help Great Britain to-day or at any other period of danger or difficulty. This consideration is the protection of our mutual trade which has heretofore been the work of British ships alone. But indeed there are many others which justify Canada in following in the footsteps of the other colonies, to answer the pressing appeal of the metropolis as has been put by several hon. members, amongst them the leader of the opposition.
What it behoves us not to forget in the present debate, and that which from my point of view, justifies the Canadian Government, apart from all matters of sentiment, in yielding to Great Britain's appeal, is the immense and increasing trade between Canada and Britain. England is our best and largest customer. Last year Great Britain purchased nine-tenths of the natural products which Canada exported. For the present, I am looking at the question from a business point of view, l am asking myself the following question. Should Canada help Great Britain in maintaining Mr. BOYER.
the empire of the sea? Outside of national sentiment, I say, yes.
