So far, Mr. Speaker, I have dealt with the trade consideration. Let us now review the various incidents which preceded the bringing down of this Bill before parliament and those which have transpired since it was laid on the table of the House. There is nothing more amusing than to review the attitude of the opposition and to analize the conduct of its leaders at each one of the various phases through which the navy question has passed so far.
Let us analyse the incidents, Now, for the first attitude. It was in November, 1909, that the hon. member for North Toronto, in order the better to show to the country his undying filial love for the mother country, as if the British authorities were neglecting or delaying the execution of a project or plan of naval defence which had been examined during the intercolonial conferences of 1897, 1902 and 1905, placed upon ' Hansard ' a spech of several hours' duration to show the absolute necessity of speedy action and of building a navy, the immediate object of which would be the protec-143i
tion of our coasts and which would also go to the assistance of the mother country in case of war, should she require our services. Finally, on the 29th of March, the right hon. the Prime Minister, acting in concert with the leader of the opposition, drafted a resolution in the folowing terms,:-
The House will cordially approve of any necessary expenditure designed to promote the speedy organization of the Canadian naval service in co-operation with and in close relation to the imperial navy, along the lines suggested by the admiralty at the Last imperial conference, and in full sympathy with the view that the naval supremacy of Britain is essential to the security of the commerc the safety of the empire, and the peace of the world.
That proposition was moved by the right hon. the Prime Minister and seconded by the hon. the leader of the opposition, and agreed to without a dissentient voice; which means that not even the voice of the hon. member for Jacques Cartier was heard against the motion. Such was the first attitude of the opposition. The second attitude was that taken in 1909.
In the year 1909, the intercolonial conference of London took place. That conference gave birth to the plan which is the object of the Bill now under consideration, the building of a Canadian navy and the British admiralty endorsed the proposition then made by the representatives of Canada. It was then that one could gather from the reading of the newspapers that the leader of the opposition, as became a good patriot such as he claimed to be, gave his approbation to this pre-eminently national policy and he professed to be in entire accord with the views of the Prime Minister as to the draught of a programme of naval defence. Thoroughly satisfied that the construction of a Canadian navy was what was most desirable in that respect he said that we would by that means discharge our duty to Great Britain, to Canada and he added:
The establishment of a Canadian navy unanimously asked for by both parties would much better answer the purpose than any gift of Dreadnoughts.
And while the leader of the opposition was thus holding forth, the hon. member for North Toronto took up the burden of- the song and in a speech delivered in the capital of Nova Scotia, said:
That we should be ready to defend our country and that a magnificent future was smiling upon us. That the creation of a Canadian navy would result in giving a fresh impetus to the shipbuilding industry and to the construction of steel ships in Canada, thus creating an enormous quantity of labo,.. and promoting an immense development.

leader of the opposition proposes nothing more nor less than that the Dominion government should send $25,000,000 to Great Britain, in order that she may buy Dreadnoughts with this money. But after all the hon. gentleman is humane, and he would feel loath at spending the people's money without giving the people a voice in the expenditure of that money; he would agree, but, of course only after the $25,000,000 have been subscribed to England, that we should refer the matter to the people, in order to know whether they want us to give more.
I could hardly give the finishing touch to this authentic description, without referring to my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier. Well, sir, I am happy to be able to state that among the leaders of the opposition who can speak with any authority, he is the only one so far who has stuck to his guns. It is true the hon. member from Jacques Cartier, like all the hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House, did approve of the resolution of the 29th March, 1909, which aimed at a speedy organization of a Canadian naval service; but he did not feel like sleeping on his laurels, and in his Lachine speech, he emphatically stated that he was opposed to any kind of contribution or marine, etc. Since then, the hon. gentleman has ever maintained the same attitude.
In another respect the hon. gentleman is entitled to credit, and that is for the manner in which he advocates a plebiscite. He wants the government to refer the matter to the people, befor any expenditure is incurred for the navy, while his leader, less exacting, would be quite satisfied, if the money were spent first. Surely the hon. gentlemen disagree as to the manner of helping Great Britain and as to the manner in which the matter should be referred to the people.
That is, sir, a very incomplete hut a truthful statement of the flagrant contradictions into which the leaders of the Conservative party in this House have fallen, since the 29th of March, 1909.
Is such conduct calculated to inspire the electorate with confidence? Is there a single hon. gentleman here, opposed on principle to the building of a navy, who could in the face of such tactics, vote down the measure introduced by the government? He could not even follow my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier in his fictitious opposition, because, if his leader has exaggerated the amount of our contribution, he himself has sinned as much in the opposite direction. That there should arise some difference of opinion as to the mode of assisting the mother country, that is easily understood; hut that we should deny her everything, especially at a time when her prestige is threatened, is inadmissible under the circumstances.

The position taken by my hon. friend (Mr. Monk) on the Naval Service Act reminds me of the attitude he took in 1905, during the second session of the legislature, when I witnessed an exhibition such as the one which is now being given us. We were then debating the Act to establish and to provide for the government of the provinces of Alberta and of Saskatchewan. The government, going even beyond the limits allowed under the British North America Act, had in the first place brought down their Bill granting to the minorities and particularly to the French Catholic element identical rights to those engaged by the English Protestant element, in the province of Quebec. The opposition which was under the same leadership as they are to-day so bitterly opposed the provisions of this Act in connealion with legislation concerning education in those provinces, that the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) had to part company with his colleagues and in order the better to explain his flight, ha moved, just as he is doing to-day, a motion unacceptable under the terms of the law, that is to say, a motion to make the French language official before the courts of the province.
Do you know what later on became of that amendment or resolution? They caused it to play a very sad part in the province of Quebec. The French Canadian speakers of the Conservative party, wherever they addressed the electorate on the hustings throughout the province took up as their theme the famous Monk resolution: ' Gentlemen would they say, behold the hon. member for Jacques Cartier was the only gentleman who stood up on the floor of the House of Commons and tried to save the French language in the two new provinces. But the Liberals voted down his motion. It is an infamous action.' The gentleman who opposed me in the county which I have the honour to represent failed to tell the electors that the hon. member for Jacques Cartier had proposed an impossibility, under the terms of the British North America Act ; he also refrained from telling them that his chief, the leader of the opposition and his followers had voted down his motion; but he was severely punished by the electors, so much so that he even lost his deposit. Now, Mr. Speaker, do you know what will happen with the present attitude of the hon. member for Jacques Cartier? At the next general elections, you will find that Conservative speakers, addressing the electors on the very same hustings will tell them that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk) is the only member from the province of Quebec who stood up on the floor of the House to oppose the establishment of a national navy and they will exclaim .that the
Liberal members from Quebec did vote down the amendment to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Jacques Cartier. But they will again omit to say that the leader1 of the opposition and the Conservative members did also vote it down.
You will find that I shall, that at the next elections Conservative speakers will themselves state in the same localities that the member from Jacques Cartier was the only member from the province of Quebec to oppose the creation of a national navy. They will claim that the Liberal members from Quebec voted against the sub-amendment submitted by the member from Jacques Cartier. But at the same time omitting to mention that the leader of the opposition and the Conservative members had also voted against it.
Whilst this comedy will" be1 enacted in Quebec, the leader of the opposition and the remainder of the Conservative phalanx will overrun the English-speaidng. provinces claiming everywhere that the government did not do its duty towards England, because its leader, the Prime Minister, who is a French Canadian, submitted to the dictates of the members of his race sitting in this House. That is their double game, and the trick is played. Later we will find the Conservative leaders taking shelter under the same umbrella, and the understanding will still continue. Such are the elements of which His Majesty's loyal opposition is actually composed. And certain persons would like the Liberal members to betray the government on the naval question, to vote with such a party!
On Friday, the 11th February, Mr. Bou-rassa published in ' le Devoir ' this significant avowal as regards to the Naval Bill:
' If it had been for a Canadian navy, for Canada's defence, under the Canadian government's authority, I would not have found fault with Article 17, neither with Article 19, not even with the whole article. Even if the executive had abused of the powers that Article 17 gives it, the fleet remained under its authority, and parliament being convened within the fifteen days, might have overridden the government's decision and recalled the ships. But it is on reading Article 18 that I saw the bottomless depth in which we were thrown without warning and by deceit. It seems to me that the point has been made quite clear by the words of the leader of the opposition himself when in his speech he arraigned the government in the following terms: That the government's propositions do not agree with the Admiralty's propositions and recommendations, inasmuch as they allow the government to refuse to unite the naval forces of Canada to those of the empire in time of war; they

are ill-advised and dangerous. In fact-many other opposition speakers apparently hold the same views. It would be idle to attempt an analysis of their different shades of sentiment.
Our fleet will be entirely under the Canadian government's control and the government cannot definitely place that fleet at the disposal of England without the ratification of parliament. Sections 18 and 19 make this quite clear:
18.	In case" of an emergency, the Governor in Council may place at the disposal of His Majesty, for general service in the Royal Navy, the naval service or any part thereof, any ships or vessels of the naval service, and the officers and seamen serving in such ships or vessels, or any officers or seamen belonging to the naval service.
19.	Whenever the Governor in Council places the naval service or any part thereof on active service, as provided in the preceding section, if parliament is then separated by such adjournment or prorogation as will not expire within ten days, a proclamation shall be issued for a meeting of parliament within fifteen days, and parliament shall accordingly meet and sit upon the day appointed by such proclamation and shall continue to sit in like manner as if it had stood adjourned or prorogued to the same day.
But let us take the trouble of referring to the Militia Bill of 1868 and we will there find section 61 which reads in a far more peremptory manner than that of the navy.
His Majesty may call out the militia or any part thereof for actual service, either within or without the Dominion, at any time whenever it appears advisable so to do by reason of war, invasion or insurrection, or danger of any of them; and the milita men when so called out for actual service, shall continue to -serve for at least one year from the date of their being called out for actual service, if required so to do, or for any longer period which Her Majesty may appoint:
Has the King ever once exercised the prerogative thus conferred upon him, before it was changed in these latter years by striking out the words: Out of the Dominion? Has the government itself ever forced a Canadian regiment to take part in the wars of the empire, without each one of its members being consenting? But it may be asked, why should the government not consent to a plebiscite?
Now, Mr. Speaker, let us be frank. Is it the government's fault if the people are not consulted on this question, or does not this fault rest with the opposition? If on the 29th March, 1909, instead of agreeing and seconding with enthusiasm the government's proposition, the leader of the opposition had asked for a plebiscite, would not Mr. BOYER.
such a policy been more reasonable than to come to-day, as does the member for Jacques Cartier, and demand that the question be referred to the people.
Why did he not state his objections at the right time, instead of giving encouragement to the government, by his adhesion to go on with their policy? It is too late now, Mr. Speaker, to ask for a plebiscite; even if the government were authorized by the constitution, they could not virtually do it, at this moment. An appeal to the people at this juncture cannot be admitted; it would be considered as an act of weakness at a time when British colonies and their naval policy towards the mother country it would be interpreted as a want of patriotism on our part. The government is the constituted authority in the land, and as such, they are bound to exercise their authority, more particularly on a question of so great importance, not only to England, which is more directly interested, but also to all other countries which hate and envy England, and which would be the first to rejoice over the least hesitation on the part of the colonies. The time is no more for a plebiscite. It should have been asked for, before the policy of the government was laid down and presented to the House.
I am opposed to a plebiscite for another important reason, besides those already given.
We live under a representative government; we are directly responsible to the people, and every five years the electorate is called upon to ratify or condemn the position taken by their representatives on the several questions that have been submitted to parliament. The people pass judgment upon their representatives at election time, when all the political questions aie fully debated on the hustings. It is on that solemn occasion that the electors make a choice of the men that are supposed to be in a position, not only to represent them with dignity and liability, but also to represent their views on the public questions of the day. During the term of a parliament the electorate cannot reasonably interefere and dictate to their representatives in this House.
The Canadian parliament is not a municipal council obliged to submit to the taxpayers every proposal entailing the expenditure of a few' hundred dollars. The constituencies and their representatives have wider attributions and the idea of submitting to the people all important questions proposed to the House for discussion would be an anomaly that the people themselves would be the first to reprove.
Let us suppose for a moment that the government accept the amendment sub-

mitted by the hon. member for Jacques Cartier and ask the people to give their verdict on the naval policy. How many members outside of the cities, would be in a position to assert that over 25 per cent of their constituents could decide on that question with a reasonable degree of competency, keeping in mind the limited -amount of information and knowledge they have on the subject. There is nothing astonishing about it. At the present moment I know for a fact that a great number of my fellow-countrymen look only at the economic side of the question, that is to. say, the expenditure it will entail, leaving aside all the wider and higher considerations.
Then, let us sup.pose that the people of the province of Quebec reject all naval policy, when the English-speaking provinces decide on the other-side, this verdict would not mean that my fellow-countrymen are not loyal to the British Crown, and that is. nevertheless, the conclusion that would be drawn from their verdict. We all know what disastrous consequences would follow for that province. We would be isolated from the rest of the confederation. The French Canadians would be an isolated group, looked upon scornfully by the population of the other provinces. We cannot have in this parliament, without great danger of our race and creed, a party not in accord with one or the other of the two recognized political parties of this country.
There is a time for everything: at every election a chance is given to the people to pass judgment upon their representatives and upon the policy they have approved or opposed during the term of their mandate. At election time the electorate become the master, and then we have a real plebiscite.
Now, Mr. Speaker, do you happen to know what is said amongst other things that I do not believe in? Supposing that we had a plebiscite, did we not hear it said, that the province of Quebec, under the guidance of the clergy, would vote against all contribution of help of any kind to England, on the ground that it would be a step toward imperialism? Did we not hear it said that the hon. member for Jacques Cartier, and an ex-member of this House, making appeal to prejudice, would stump the province, would make a canvas from house to house, would knock at the door of every vicarage and would preach the rebellion, shielding their political aspirations behind the Catholic clergy?
That is what is being 3aid, Mr. Speaker. 1 need not say that I energetically and emphatically denounce all such slanders and calumnies, specially in so far as they are directed against the Catholic clergy of the province of Quebec. The past history of this country is there to teach us what valuable services the Catholic clergy have given to the British Crown in the hours of need, and how they would to-day as in the past, preach devotion and loyalty to the British flag under whose folds we have lived happy and free.
Moreover, is it not that same clergy that assisted in the re-election of Sir George Etienne Cartier, when he came before the electorate with his Militia Bill?
Sir, I have not the mission to defend the clergy of the province of Quebec against certain insinuations that have seemed directed against it in some places. My confidence is strong enough in that clergy, and I admire so much those who direct it, that I can't help saying here, in this House, that the clergy would not pursue such course. There is a tendency to make people believe that if we had a plebiscite, we should be surprised of the mass of English citizens who would be against all contribution to England, direct or indirect.
Well, Sir, I do not believe in this badly calculated prediction, if I may judge by the countenance of this House. Here, all the members are unanimous in having Canada contribute to the defence of the British empire. And, even the' opposition expresses a desire to do more than is proposed by the government. On the other hand, all the prominent Englishmen, the large and small journals of the country, are for one or the other policy except, perhaps a few individuals.
Some take pleasure in saying that the English farmers'do not agree with the idea of creating a national marine, nor of directly contributing for the defence of England. Here, let us be fair towards them. I may for a moment admit that they would not like to see money spent that way, but as to pretend that their greediness would speak higher than their patriotism, I say that is an injury to their address. So, the best proof that the English farmers are not antipathic to the policy, is seen in the two following facts: Lately, at Toronto, there was a convention of the ' Dominion Grange.' The president of the association at the beginning of the meeting spoke, I may say quietly, but cursing war and brining forth the idea that Canada should not spend a penny for war. Some of the members wanted to convert the opinion of the president into a motion, but the discussion became so hot that it was not thought wise to invite the votes.
Not much later, the ' grain growers ' had a convention at Prince Albert, Saskatchewan; there was on the bill a resolution in favour of a direct contribution to English marine by Canada.
It was decided not to discuss this question, because it was not in accordance with the object of the association. Here are

two facts, Sir, that are quite contrary to the idea conveyed that the English farmers are antipathic to the mother country. Supposing that we have to face a real crisis, that our territory and our coasts need defence and that our dignity as well as our interests command that we should at once make ready for self defence; all these thoughts are not suggested by what I just said, but by the reflection that such a subject must bring to every mind. But, these considerations do not cover that ground. We must take a higher standpoint, and perhaps this will help us to understand our duty in this case, always possible, that a storm may break over our heads before we can accomplish all the necessary work of resistance. We are here on the Canadian land the offsprings of two great countries, rivals for a long time, to-day together and friends to defend against the possible aggression which would be principally the result of circumstances than bad will; but, even then just as dangerous.
France and England have the duty to defend oneself. What each want to keep is their territory their riches and their civilization, but it is also and before all their spirit itself which would be apt to disappear with the invasion and remain for men only as a great souvenir, such as are to-day the Greek and Roman spirit.
So. this spirit, this civilization, the languages which are the expression of fit are ours also. We are interested to keep them intact and we could not view with indifference a war by which either of these would be in danger. We would feel morally concerned in such a cause, with all our might, our resources, and even our blood.
We would be, we are in solidarity here, and this circumstance will not only bring us closer to our forefathers' countries, but they will unite us better together. It is perhans a means of creating a durable sympathy, a fraternity between the two Canadian races.
This sentiment does not exist actually, we are bound to declare. We live peacefully, but without sympathy, for we know very little of one another, and each group has his pretensions that the other refuses to admit. The politicians. remark this wrong with sadness, and it will not soon disappear since it must do so without abdication.
If, on the other hand, each group could add to the love of the Canadian home which tends to bring them closer, the sentiment of their solidarity in the defence of a still more elevated ideal if this is possible, and for which each group concerned would be ready to sacrifice verv much, the unity would become easier and nearer; the result might be a real alliance which would add some day to the rich bunch of civilization, a new variety formed of the two prettiest

and most ancient flowers which compose it. Let us not fear to take strong determinations.
Let us enter, without any mental reservation, upon the new path pointed out to us by honour and duty, as well as by the well understood interests of Canada for the present as for the future.
